blocks.text: --- name: adversarial-review description: > Adversarial code review of changes to swarm-scheduler-exporter — working tree, staged diff, a branch vs master, a commit range, or a PR — in any language (Rust, bash, Dockerfile, Makefile, YAML, docs). Uses user-level Rust skills for Rust and Cargo paths, checks the exporter's invariants (read-only Docker access, metrics as a public contract, series lifecycle, single reconciler owner, bounded work, release pipeline) and reports ranked findings with a block/approve verdict. Use when the user asks to review changes, a diff, a PR or a branch, to "check my work before committing", whether it "is ready to merge", or to "poke holes in this" — even if they don't name a language or say the word "review". ---

You are a hostile reviewer. Assume the change is **wrong until proven right**: it hides a bug, breaks an invariant, or drifts from a contract. Your job is to find the specific input, state, or path where it fails — not to praise it, not to restyle it. A review that finds nothing is only credible after you have actively tried to break the code and failed.
This skill routes to the user-level Rust skills and the project's authorities rather than replacing them. Read `AGENTS.md` first: its rules are the review's floor.

When invoked directly: review the scope the user gives (`gh pr view <n>` for intent, then `gh pr diff <n>`); with none, the uncommitted work (`git diff HEAD` plus untracked files, which no diff shows); on a clean tree, `git diff master...HEAD`. Never review from a description of the change.

Read the stated **intent** (`git log --oneline` for the range, any linked issue or PR body): a change that works but does something other than what it claims is a finding. Read every changed file in full, not just the hunks, and for non-trivial changes the callers, implementations, tests and docs of what changed, found with a reference search, not assumed from the diff: a signature or behavior change is only safe if every call site agrees.

For any `**/*.rs` path, any `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `clippy.toml`, `rustfmt.toml` or `rust-toolchain.toml`, use user-level Rust skills and read `AGENTS.md`; project rules are findings even when clippy is green. Every other path (Dockerfile, compose files, `Makefile`, `.mk/*.mk`, GitHub workflows, other YAML, bash, Markdown) gets the passes below plus the repository invariants with the **same rigor** — an unmatched language is not a lighter review.
A meta-test under `meta/tests/` guards a claim nothing else checks; "Meta-tests must not pass on nothing" under the invariants says how to attack one.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: These are the ways this exporter breaks that generic reviewers miss.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
Commit type matches whether it ships
blocks.text: `svu` derives the release from the Conventional Commits since the last tag, and pull requests land as merge commits, so every commit in the range counts. A change to the binary or the image that users should receive typed `chore`, `docs`, `perf` or `refactor` never ships; tooling typed `fix` or `feat` cuts a release with nothing in it; a stray `!` cuts a major; and a word ending in `fix` or `feat` right before a colon anywhere in a subject counts as that type (`AGENTS.md`, `docs/release.md`).

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
Read-only against Docker — enforced in code, not at runtime
blocks.text: The exporter must only ever *read* from the Docker API. A `:ro` bind of `/var/run/docker.sock` does **not** make the API read-only: `:ro` only stops the container from modifying the socket file, and a client can still POST creates, updates and removes through it. So the read-only property rests entirely on the code:

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)

blocks.text: `DockerApi` (`src/docker`), on a `Client` over rust-common's docker-client (bollard) built without its `attach` feature, which exposes only list, inspect and events calls (nodes, services, a service inspect, tasks, containers, a container inspect, events), and through which all collector code reaches Docker;

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)

A diff that loosens any of those rules, or reaches Docker around the client, is a finding.

blocks.text: docs claiming that `:ro` makes the socket read-only. The README's Security section says the exporter only *issues* read requests and that enforcing it needs a proxy; a diff that walks that back is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
Read-only against Docker — enforced in code, not at runtime
blocks.text: Runtime enforcement needs an authorization proxy in front of the socket. The repo ships one example, `deployments/docker/docker-compose.socket-proxy.yaml` with its allowlist `socket-proxy.env`, pinned by `TestSocketProxy_ExampleAllowlist` against the real proxy image. It makes the API read-only, not least-privilege: the proxy's ACL is per path prefix, so the `SERVICES` and `TASKS` the exporter needs also allow service and task logs, and `CONTAINERS=1` allows every `GET` under `/containers` (logs, archive, export). Docs that call it least-privilege or exact per endpoint, an allowlist line relying on an image default, or a change to `socket-proxy.env` without the test still passing are findings.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: Dashboards and alerts key on metric names and label sets. A renamed metric, or a label added, removed or renamed, is a finding unless `docs/metrics.md` (and any alert example in `docs/alerts.md` that uses it) changes in the same diff — and even then, call out the break for existing users. A label fed by an unbounded value (container or task IDs, timestamps, free-form strings) is a cardinality finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: Removing a resource **deletes** its series (`GaugeVec::delete`, `delete_service_series`); it never sets them to 0. A stale zero series tells dashboards the resource still exists. A service whose label identity changes (stack, name, mode, a custom label) has its old series deleted before the new ones appear.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: A known state set (task states, update states, container states) is emitted exhaustively for every subject, zeros included, so absent series never mean "0".

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: A family that mirrors a dynamic set (`replicas_state`, `running_replicas`, `at_desired`, `nodes_by_state`, `container_state`) is a snapshot collector: the whole set is built first and published in one swap, so a scrape never sees it empty or half-written. A build error keeps the previous set. Resetting a `GaugeVec` and setting it again is a finding: a scrape can land in between.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The service and node caches and the gauges derived from them are written by exactly one task, the reconciler (`src/collector/reconciler`). Everything else only asks it for work or for a snapshot:

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The event listener only marks keys dirty (`ReconcilerHandle::enqueue_event`), never blocking and never calling Docker. A cache or gauge written from the listener, the poller or an HTTP handler is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The dirty set, the generations and the resync counters share one lock (`Shared::state`), where 1.x had two with a lock order. It is never held across an `.await`, and nothing takes a second lock while holding it; a guard alive across an await point or a new nested lock is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: A generation (service, node, and the epoch for resyncs) is bumped when a change is *queued*, not when it is applied, so a queued, unapplied change already invalidates a poll. Moving a bump to apply time is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: Readiness is the first completed resync: the poller does not start and `/healthz` stays `503` ("initial resync not completed") until then. A resync fetches both the service list and the node list before mutating anything, and a failed one mutates nothing.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: A resync is requested on overflow, on retry exhaustion, on a recovered panic, on every event-stream reconnect and every `PERIODIC_RESYNC_INTERVAL`. Dropping any of these leaves the caches behind Docker with nothing to catch them up.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
A panic costs a step, not the process
blocks.text: Each reconciler step runs under `catch_unwind` (`reconciler/recover.rs`), logs `reconciler recovered from panic` with the payload and a backtrace, and requests a rate-limited resync; `collector::must` panics on purpose for label values that do not fit their family, as the Prometheus client's `With` does, relying on that recovery. Findings: switching the release profile to `panic = "abort"`, a step that holds a lock or a half-applied change across the point where it can panic, a panic path that skips the resync, and a `catch_unwind` around code that is not a whole step.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: `clippy.toml` bans `Timestamp::now`, `Zoned::now`, `SystemTime::now` and `std::time::Instant::now`; the time comes only through `clock::Clock`, whose one wall-clock read (`SystemClock`) lives in rust-common, so this repository has no exemption for them. An `#[expect(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` for a clock read, a ban entry removed, or a time read that bypasses the `Clock` (a timestamp gauge, a staleness check) is a finding: the tests drive health and timestamps with tokio's paused clock and would no longer see the code. `tokio::time::Instant` is allowed because it follows the paused clock.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: `clippy.toml` also bans `std::process::Command::new` and `tokio::process::Command::new`: the exporter spawns no process. Only a test, meta-test or harness function that runs a program (the built exporter, `make`, `kill`) carries an `#[expect(clippy::disallowed_methods)]` for it, with its reason; one on code under `src/` outside a test module is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The poller counts tasks against an immutable snapshot it gets from the reconciler and hands the counts back; the reconciler publishes a service only if its generation, its dirty key, the epoch and (for global services and global jobs) the node generation and the pending node refresh all still match the snapshot. A rejected service keeps its last published series for at most `MAX_CARRIED_POLLS` (2) polls, only with an unchanged label identity; then its series are omitted and the poll fails, so health turns red. Findings:

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: counting or deduplicating tasks from the live caches instead of the snapshot;

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: a new rejection reason not checked, or carry-over that is unbounded or crosses a label identity change;

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: `mark_poll_ok` on anything but a fully published poll;

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: a poll or snapshot exchange that sends or waits without also selecting on its cancellation token, or a reply channel without room for the answer, so a shutdown can hang the worker join past `SHUTDOWN_BUDGET`.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: Events become dirty keys in a bounded set (`PENDING_KEY_CAP`, 4096); past the cap the set is dropped with fresh allocations and a resync is requested instead. The reconciler inspects at most `SERVICE_KEYS_PER_CYCLE` (32) keys per cycle, a failed inspect is retried after `SERVICE_RETRY_DELAYS` and then dropped for a resync, and a failed resync or node refresh backs off up to `BACKOFF_MAX_DELAY`. A task per event, an unbounded channel, or a retry without a delay is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: Every request/response Docker call runs under `with_docker_timeout` (`DOCKER_REQUEST_TIMEOUT`, 15s) and the shutdown token. The event stream is the one exception: it has no deadline and is cancelled per connection on reconnect and on shutdown. Container enrichment shares one deadline per poll and at most `CONTAINERS_INSPECT_CAP` (300) inspects, failures included.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: No unbounded task spawning, and no map keyed by an external ID (service, node, container, task) without an eviction path when that resource disappears; that includes the reconciler's generation and retry maps.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The health snapshot (`src/collector/health.rs`) is evaluated at scrape time, by `/healthz` and by the `swarm_exporter_health` `GaugeFunc` alike. It is unhealthy until the first resync completes, until a poll has been published, when the last published poll is older than `max(3 × poll delay, 30s)`, and when a requested resync has been outstanding for longer than that window. A health signal set by the poller itself, a timestamp moved on a failed or partial publish, or a reason string in `docs/operations.md` that no longer matches the code is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The HTTP server keeps its two deadlines (`server::HEADER_READ_TIMEOUT` 5s and `server::WRITE_STALL_TIMEOUT` 15s in `src/server.rs`), enforced per connection by service-kit's server, and a drain bounded by the shared shutdown deadline. Removing one, or serving a connection outside `service_kit::http::serve`, is a finding.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: `/metrics` and `/healthz` take no input that becomes work: no query parameter, header or body may trigger a Docker call, widen a scrape, or allocate per request beyond the exposition itself.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
blocks.text: The image runs the static base as an explicit non-root `USER`, with every dhi.io base pinned by tag; the release job publishes only the digest it smoke-tested and scanned. If the diff touches the Dockerfile, the compose files, `.trivyignore.yaml`, a workflow, `scripts/image-test.sh` or `docs/release.md`, read [references/release-and-image.md](references/release-and-image.md) and walk its items: they are part of this section.

heading_path: Repository invariants (check on every review, whatever changed)
Meta-tests must not pass on nothing
blocks.text: A meta-test guards a claim nothing else checks: the toolchain pins and the vacuous flags (`meta/tests/toolchain.rs`), the Dockerfile's frontend and bases (`dockerfiles.rs`), the Docker boundary (`docker_boundary.rs`) and the workspace lints (`workspace_lints.rs`). Run the vacuity pass on every one the diff touches, or whose input the diff changes: try to make the guarded thing go wrong and see whether the test still notices. A test that passes because its walk found no file, its regex matched nothing or its rule never ran is a false pass. Every rule needs a negative control that fails on a planted violation, and a non-empty-input assertion. A change that loosens one — a wider allowlist, a narrower walk, a dropped negative control, a pattern that no longer matches the file it reads — is a finding unless it says why.

Beyond the generic passes (logic, nil and empty input, aliasing, error handling, concurrency, resources, security), run these with a "how would I make this fail" framing, and name one concrete failing input per candidate rather than asserting "looks fine".
**Contract drift:** a public signature, flag, environment variable, output format, exit code or error text changed without updating every consumer and the docs (*Docs drift* below).

**Tests:** a test that passes against the *old* code, that asserts on a fake's recorded calls instead of the behavior they produced, or that was weakened or deleted to make the change pass is a finding. A bug fix with no regression test is a gap worth flagging.
The passes above are shaped by the diff. These run on **every** review, whatever changed.

Ask the one question the endpoint and image rules in the invariants are built on: does this change create a new place where something from outside becomes work — a request parameter that becomes a Docker call, a label value that becomes a series, an event that becomes a task — or does it make the image or its deployment more privileged? If it does, walk the "Endpoint and image hardening" (including its reference) and "Bounded work" items against it.

A diff that removes a user-visible surface — a metric, a label, a flag, an environment variable, a health behavior — and in the same breath rewrites that surface's test to assert it is *absent* must cite the specification line that retired it. The specification here is `docs/metrics.md`, `docs/configuration.md` (Flags, Environment) and the Health section of `docs/operations.md`. A commit message is not a specification, and a page that still documents the surface means the removal is unspecified.

A test flipped from "X happens" to "X does not happen" is not evidence that X should go — it is the deletion wearing the test's clothes. Ask, in order: which spec line retires this surface, and does it change in this diff? If none, this is a **critical** finding whatever the diff's stated intent was. If one exists, is the diff removing exactly what that line retires and no more?

heading_path: (c) A new suppression has to show its work
blocks.text: Any new `#[expect(...)]`, `# shellcheck disable=` or `# droast ignore=` is a standing decision to let a linter stay silent, and nothing but the reviewer judges the reason. So demand the attempt: for `too_many_lines`, was the obvious extraction tried and what broke? For a cast lint, why is the range safe? For `struct_excessive_bools`, why is an enum wrong here? A suppression whose reason comment restates the rule instead of explaining why the fix does not apply is a finding, and so is a suppression with no reason comment at all. The same holds for a new `allow` in `[workspace.lints]` or `clippy.toml` — and a lint setting there that matches nothing in this repo (copied from another project) is a finding too.

Before accepting a new helper, search for the one that already exists — in `src/**`, `tests/support`, `testenv/**` and rust-common's crates (a local copy of a helper rust-common has is a finding), by *behavior*, not by the name the author chose. Check label building and sanitization, metric constants, formatting, test fakes and wait helpers. Two implementations of the same rule drift apart, and the one the reviewer did not read is the one that keeps the bug.
The configuration and metrics contracts are written down more than once and can disagree silently.
A flag added or changed in `src/cli.rs` needs its entry in the Flags section of `docs/configuration.md` (clap's `--help` output), with the same name, default and meaning.
The same holds for the Docker client environment variables in its Environment section and for the metric list in `docs/metrics.md`.
A surface the code has and the docs do not mention is a finding; so is a documented one nothing implements, and so is a default in the docs that differs from the code.

Do not re-run the repository's gates (`make verify`, `make check`, `make rust-deny`, `make test-integration`, `cargo test -p meta`, `make docker-build`, `make rust-release-binaries`, `make image-build-test`). The implementer is expected to run them and CI runs them again, but do not assume either happened: report the verification evidence you actually have (under adversarial-review-loop, `verification.txt` when supplied, which is the implementer's claim and not proof; when invoked directly, the CI status or gate output in the PR or session) and what is missing, such as a `src/collector`, `src/docker` or `testenv` change with no integration run reported. A failure in that evidence caused by the change is a confirmed finding. Never say that a check you did not see passed, and a skipped test is not a pass: the integration runner prints `SKIP` for a test it could not run. Judge whether the change's tests prove it: a behaviour change needs a test that fails on the old code. When invoked directly, one focused test (`cargo test --lib collector::reconciler::tests::<name>`, or `cargo test --test engine_wire <name>`) may be run to confirm a single suspected finding, never a full suite or gate. A candidate that is neither reproduced nor traced end to end is dropped: a vague "consider" is not a finding.
Facts the evidence has to be read against:

Which gates a changed path owes is `AGENTS.md`'s *Validation matrix*: a changed path with none of its rows in the evidence is missing evidence. A gate that was impractical (no Docker daemon for the DinD Swarm `make test-integration` needs, no network for cargo-deny) is unverified, not passed.
A change to `.github/workflows/release.yaml` has no end-to-end check but a release dry run: say which steps could not be exercised.

Rank by severity, worst first. Nothing is more important than a genuine correctness or read-only-invariant break: those are normally **critical**. Skip pure formatting the linters already catch unless it changes meaning or breaks a required gate. For each finding:

<path>:<line> — <severity: critical | high | medium | low>: <one-line defect>
  Failure: <the concrete input/state → the wrong result or broken invariant>
  Fix: <the specific change>

Findings first, then open questions or assumptions, then a one-line verdict: **block**, **approve with nits**, or **approve**, and one line: `Verification evidence: seen … / missing …`. If you found nothing, state what you tried to break so the "no findings" is credible. Be blunt; do not soften a real defect to be polite, and do not invent findings to look thorough.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: Every base is pinned by tag, deliberately not by digest, since dhi.io rebuilds its tags too often to follow by digest: the build stage (`dhi.io/rust:…-debian13-dev`) and the shared `base` stage (`dhi.io/static:…`). The `# syntax=` frontend line is pinned by tag and index digest. A base on `latest` or with no tag, a digest pin on a dhi.io base, a frontend without a digest, a build-stage Rust release that differs from `rust-toolchain.toml` and the workflows' toolchain steps (patch included), or a zig, cargo-zigbuild or `rust-std` download without its sha256 check, is a finding.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: Two targets share the `base` stage, which sets the explicit `USER 65532:65532` (never root, so the uid is pinned in the Dockerfile rather than inherited from the base image's default), the port, the `--healthcheck` `HEALTHCHECK` and the entrypoint: `runtime`, the default, whose build stage cross-compiles the binary, and `prebuilt`, which CI and the release build and which must COPY the release asset from the `dist` build context unchanged, so the image binary stays byte-identical to it (`scripts/image-test.sh` checks the sha256, `meta/tests/dockerfiles.rs` the stages).

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: A diff must not make this worse: adding root, removing or changing the explicit `USER`, dropping the static base, adding a shell or package manager to the base stage, or widening mounts and capabilities in the compose files is a finding. Socket access is granted by adding the socket's group (`--group-add`, `user: "65532:<gid>"`), not by running as root.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: `docs/release.md` is the contract; `.github/workflows/release.yaml` implements it. Tags here are immutable, so the order of the release job is the safety property:

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: The mode is decided from two fail-closed lookups before anything is pushed: the Git tag on the remote and `ghcr.io/…:<version>`. Only "not found" may read as absent; a lookup whose error is treated as absence is critical.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: The release runs no test suite of its own: `ci-green` (`require-ci-green`) gates on CI's `ci-result` and on `integration.yaml`'s `integration` for the push of the exact commit; CI's `image` job builds the release binaries with `make rust-release-binaries` and the `prebuilt` target from them, and runs the full image suite on amd64 and the reduced one on arm64 (`docs/release.md`, "What CI proves"). A change that weakens CI's `image` or `rust` job, or the integration suite, or lets one skip on a push, weakens the release and is a finding.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: The `audit` job (cargo-deny) runs alongside the release job's build; `require-job-success` waits for it before the first step that publishes. A publishing step moved above that wait, or the wait made conditional, is a finding.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: The image is built once, from the binaries the release built (or the published ones `release-mode` verified), into the job-local registry, smoke-tested, and only the digest that was scanned is copied to GHCR (`skopeo copy --all --preserve-digests`), checked by hashing what GHCR serves, attested and signed, and only then tagged `:<version>`. A second image build, a scan of anything but the published digest, a copy that can change the digest (the build forces gzip layers for this reason), or a version tag added before attest and sign is a finding.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: A reused image is verified by attestation and signature, never by comparing a rebuilt index.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: The scan is `trivy-gate`, at the latest Trivy (never pinned), failing on fixable `HIGH` and `CRITICAL` findings (`--ignore-unfixed` by design). Exceptions live only in `.trivyignore.yaml`, each scoped to paths or purls, with a `statement` and an `expired_at`; a lowered severity, a Trivy pin or an exception anywhere else is a finding.

heading_path: Image, release and CI invariants — swarm-scheduler-exporter
blocks.text: Workflow tokens are `contents: read` at the top of every workflow, and a job asks for more only with a comment saying why. Every action is pinned to a full commit SHA and every image a workflow runs to an index digest; a new floating `@v…` or `:tag` is a finding.

The full list, with what counts as a finding, is in `.agents/skills/adversarial-review/SKILL.md`, "Repository invariants". The ones to keep in mind while writing code:

**Read-only against Docker, enforced in code.** A `:ro` socket bind does not make the API read-only. `DockerApi` exposes list, inspect and events calls only, and `src/docker` makes only the bollard read calls (the version negotiation's `GET /version` included), with `docker-client`'s `attach` feature off. `meta/tests/docker_boundary.rs` holds it there: no manifest enables that feature, only `src/docker` names the crate (and bollard, as `docker_client::bollard`) and builds no request of its own, the calls are only reads whose sections the shipped socket-proxy allowlist grants, and bollard (which the harness creates and removes things with) is declared directly only by the harness, outside the exporter package.

**Metrics are the public contract.** A renamed metric or a changed label set updates `docs/metrics.md` (and any alert example in `docs/alerts.md`) in the same change. No label fed by an unbounded value.
**Series lifecycle.** A removed resource's series are deleted, never set to 0; known state sets are emitted exhaustively; snapshot families are built whole and swapped in one step.

**One owner for Swarm state.** Only the reconciler task writes the caches and derived gauges; the event dispatcher only marks keys dirty through a `ReconcilerHandle`. The dirty set, the generations and the resync counters share one lock (`Shared::state`), never held across an `.await`.

**A panic costs a step, not the process.** Each reconciler step runs under `catch_unwind` (`reconciler/recover.rs`), logs `reconciler recovered from panic` and requests a resync, which is why the release profile keeps `panic = "unwind"`.
**Bounded work.** Bounded dirty-key set, bounded inspects per cycle, retries with delays, every request under `with_docker_timeout`, and no map keyed by an external ID without an eviction path.

**The clock is injected.** `clippy.toml` bans `Timestamp::now`, `Zoned::now`, `SystemTime::now` and `std::time::Instant::now`; the time comes from the `Clock` trait, so tests drive it with tokio's paused clock. The time comes only through `clock::Clock`; the one wall-clock read is clock's `SystemClock`, in rust-common, so the exporter has no `disallowed_methods` exemption for it.

**No child process.** `clippy.toml` also bans `std::process::Command::new` and `tokio::process::Command::new`: the exporter spawns nothing. The tests, meta-tests and harness functions that run a program carry an `#[expect(clippy::disallowed_methods, reason = "...")]` each.
**Health means published data.** The health snapshot is evaluated at scrape time; nothing marks health from the poller itself.

The version strings come from `SWARM_SCHEDULER_EXPORTER_VERSION`, `_COMMIT` and `_DATE` at compile time (`src/version.rs`, `service_kit::buildinfo!`); unset, they read `dev`, `none` and `unknown`, and an empty one stays empty. `make rust-dist` and `make rust-run` set them from git; `make rust-release-binaries` from rust.mk's `GIT_VERSION`, `GIT_COMMIT` and `BUILD_DATE`, which the release sets to the tag, the commit's first seven characters and its commit date; and the Dockerfile's build stage from its `VERSION`, `COMMIT` and `DATE` arguments, which also fill the image labels. The binary has no `--version`: it logs them in its startup line and exports them as `swarm_exporter_build_info`.
Lints are silenced only with `#[expect(lint, reason = "...")]`: `allow_attributes` is denied, the reason is mandatory, and an `#[expect]` that stops firing fails the build.
Fixtures under `testdata/` are captures (Engine API objects, golden files); the whitespace pre-commit hooks skip them, so do not tidy them by hand.

**Jobs:** every job sets `timeout-minutes` (a composite action cannot time out its own steps). Every checkout that pushes nothing sets `persist-credentials: false`; the release's checkout sets it too, and its tag push passes the token to that one `git push`. Every job that holds a write permission or `id-token` runs in the `release` environment.

**Concurrency:** CI (and `integration.yaml`) groups a pull request's runs by `${{ github.workflow }} @ <head label>` and cancels the older one; every other run (a push to the default branch, a dispatch) gets its own group, `${{ github.run_id }}`, because GitHub keeps one pending run per group and the release gate needs CI on the exact commit (see `ci.yaml`). A warm-up uses `<name>-${{ github.ref }}`, never a static group. The release uses the one `release` group and is never cancelled.

**Caches:** the default branch is the only writer, because every pull request can restore its caches and the default branch cannot restore a pull request's. The pre-commit cache is saved only by `pre-commit-warmup.yaml`; CI restores it with `actions/cache/restore` under the same key, `pre-commit|<OS>|<resolved Python version>|<hash of .pre-commit-config.yaml>`, so CI sets up the warm-up's `python_version` and installs its pre-commit version. The Rust cache is `Swatinem/rust-cache` with `shared-key: ci`, saved on `master` only (the `image` job under its own `key: static`, `integration.yaml` under `key: integration`); the release writes its own, `prefix-key: release`. No image build uses a layer cache: the prebuilt target is the base plus one COPY.
**pre-commit** is pinned to the same version in CI, the warm-up and the `gha-pre-commit-reviewdog-actions` jobs (their `pre-commit-version` input).

**Release:** `release.yaml` is a `workflow_dispatch` with an optional `version` and a `dry_run`, built from gh-composite-actions (`release-version`, `require-ci-green`, `release-mode`, `toolchain-record`, `toolchain-recover`, `check-pinned-bases`, `trivy-gate`, `binary-attestation-status`, `setup-zigbuild`, `setup-cargo-deny`). svu derives the version from the commits only when none is given, and is installed only then, so a version entered by hand releases even when GitHub's release downloads fail. All commits MUST be Conventional Commits 1.0.0 **with a scope**: `<type>(<scope>)[!]: <description>`, optional blank-line body and footers. Enforced by the `conventional-pre-commit` `commit-msg` hook (`--force-scope`) and by the `conventional-commits` CI job. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `test`, `refactor`, `perf`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `style`, `revert`. Breaking changes use `!` before `:` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer. Release notes are not built from these messages: `gh release create --generate-notes` lists the merged pull requests by title. Examples: `fix(collector): drop stale task metrics when a service is removed`, `ci(release): pin trivy`.
Release versions are derived by `svu` from the commits since the last tag, so a wrong type ships a wrong version:
Release | Commit | Example
major | any type with `!` before the colon, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer | `feat(metrics)!: rename the replica gauges`
minor | `feat` | `feat(collector): add node labels`
patch | `fix` | `fix(collector): skip removed services`
none | everything else: `perf`, `refactor`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `docs`, `style`, `test`, `revert` | `perf(collector): ...`
The highest bump among the commits wins; with only "none" commits since the last tag, a release with no version fails with "nothing to bump".

**Pick the type by whether the change should ship, not by what kind of change it is.** Anything that changes the shipped binary or image and that users should receive is `fix` (or `feat`), even when it is a performance improvement, a refactor or a revert. Use `perf`, `refactor`, `style` and `revert` only when the commit is deliberately not meant to trigger a release on its own. A `revert` of a shipped `feat` or `fix` is itself a `fix`. `svu` matches `feat`/`fix` anywhere in the subject (e.g. `prefix:` counts as `fix:`), so avoid a word ending in `feat` or `fix` directly before a colon in other subjects. PRs land as merge commits, so every commit counts, not just the PR title. See [`docs/release.md`](docs/release.md).

`make test-integration` builds the release binary and runs it against a throwaway Swarm: one manager and two workers, each a privileged `docker:dind` container on your Docker daemon, joined over a dedicated bridge network. The harness is the `testenv` crate, with the Docker SDK behind its `integration` feature, and the suite is its `integration` test target (`testenv/tests/integration`), a runner of its own (`harness = false`): one cluster for the whole run, the tests one after another, since they share the cluster and several of them disrupt its nodes. A plain `cargo test` never builds it, because the target requires the `integration` feature; that is what keeps the ordinary test run free of Docker. The same suite runs on every pull request (`.github/workflows/integration.yaml`).

A new test is a function in one of the modules under `testenv/tests/integration`, registered by name in the `TESTS` table of `main.rs`; the names keep the `TestArea_Behaviour` form, so a `RUN` pattern selects them the way it always has.

Prerequisites: a Docker daemon that allows privileged containers. The host may itself be a Swarm node: the test Swarm lives entirely inside the DinD containers, and nothing on the host daemon is touched except the labelled containers and network the run creates and removes. The nodes never pull from a registry: the workload image is pulled once on the host and loaded into each of them.

make test-integration                            # the whole suite
make test-integration RUN='^TestNode_'           # only the tests matching a regexp
make test-integration UPDATE=1 RUN=TestSnapshot_ # rewrite the golden file under testenv/tests/integration/testdata

`RUN` takes the patterns of Go's `-run` flag rather than libtest's substring filter: a regular expression per `/`-separated level (`'^TestSocketProxy_ExampleAllowlist/denied'`), unanchored, with a top-level `|` separating whole alternatives (`'^TestNode_Drain$|^TestService_'`). A pattern that selects no test fails the run instead of passing it, so a typo cannot certify coverage, and the run prints how many tests it selected. Each test and subtest prints a `--- PASS`, `--- FAIL` or `--- SKIP` line with its duration, then the run prints the selected, passed, skipped and failed counts (`[it] 22 selected, 22 passed, 0 skipped, 0 failed`): a skipped test is not counted as passed. `SSE_IT_BINARY` names another binary to test instead of the release build.

`SSE_IT_KEEP_ON_FAILURE=true` keeps the cluster running when bring-up or a test fails, and prints the manager's address (`DOCKER_HOST=tcp://127.0.0.1:<port> docker node ls`) and the command that removes it. Every resource of such a run carries `swarm-scheduler-exporter.it.keep=true`, so no later run's sweep removes it: only that command or `make sweep-test-leaks` does.

`SSE_IT_WORKERS` changes the number of workers, `SSE_IT_DIND_IMAGE` the `docker:dind` image, and `SSE_IT_SUITE_TIMEOUT` (default `12m`) the deadline after which every waiting test fails and teardown runs.

Every container and network a run creates carries the `swarm-scheduler-exporter.it.envid` label. At start-up the run logs a cleanup command for its own resources (`docker ps -aq --filter label=swarm-scheduler-exporter.it.envid=<id> | xargs -r docker rm -fv; …`), so a run killed half-way can still be cleaned up by hand. Each run also removes the environments of earlier runs that are abandoned: older than an hour (`SSE_IT_STALE_AFTER`, a Go duration), and owned (the `swarm-scheduler-exporter.it.owner` label, `<hostname>:<pid>`, and the `.pidns` label) by a process on this host, in this PID namespace, that no longer exists. An environment of another host, of a run still going, of a run started with `SSE_IT_KEEP_ON_FAILURE`, or without readable owner and start labels is kept, and the reason is logged. `make sweep-test-leaks` removes every labelled environment, whatever its age or owner — do not run it while another run is in progress.

Release notes are not built from these messages: `gh release create --generate-notes` lists the merged pull requests by title.
Common types: `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `test`, `refactor`, `perf`, `build`, `ci`, `chore`, `style`, `revert`. Use a lower-case, imperative description:

fix(collector): drop stale task metrics when a service is removed
fix(deps): bump the Docker client to pick up an upstream fix
feat(metrics)!: rename the replica gauges
Mark breaking changes with `!` before the colon or a `BREAKING CHANGE: <description>` footer.

The release version is derived from these types: since the last release, any `feat` makes the next release a minor, any `fix` a patch, and `!` or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer a major; `build`, `chore`, `ci`, `docs`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style` and `test` bump nothing. See [`docs/release.md`](docs/release.md).

Pick the type by whether the change should ship, not by what kind of change it is. A performance improvement, a refactor or a revert that changes the shipped binary or image and that users should receive is a `fix` (or a `feat`). Use `perf`, `refactor`, `style` and `revert` only when the commit is deliberately not meant to trigger a release on its own.

Pull requests are merged with merge commits; squash and rebase merging are disabled. Every commit in a pull request therefore lands on `master` as it is and counts toward the version, so each commit needs a correct type, not just the pull request as a whole. The `conventional-commits` CI job checks every one of them. Enabling squash merging would make the pull-request title the commit subject instead, and would need a CI check on pull-request titles first.

Prometheus exporter for Docker Swarm focused on **task state visibility**, **accurate desired replicas**, and **operability at scale**. Fork of (and huge thanks to) **[akerouanton/swarm-tasks-exporter](https://github.com/akerouanton/swarm-tasks-exporter)**.

**Swarm Scheduler Exporter** surfaces what Docker Swarm’s **scheduler** is doing right now, and *why*. It reports **desired replicas** (including accurate eligibility for `global` services), **live task state** per service (current task per slot, or per node for `global` services), **service update/rollback** state + timestamps, **cluster node** availability, and now **SLO-friendly service readiness** signals.

Watches Swarm **service** and **node** events to keep metrics fresh: events only mark what changed, and a single reconciler inspects it, backed by a full resync (service and node list) at startup, every 5 minutes, whenever it had to drop changes, and every time the event stream reconnects. A node-only refresh also runs about every minute to keep node and manager status fresh. Event stream details: [docs/operations.md](docs/operations.md#event-stream-and-refresh).
Periodically polls **tasks** and aggregates **current** states per service (current task per slot for replicated services or per node for global services, exhaustive zero-emission).
Computes **desired replicas** precisely for `global` services (eligible nodes only: status/availability/constraints/platforms).
Emits **exporter** and **cluster** health metrics for alerting & SLOs.
Sanitizes and validates **custom labels** for Prometheus compliance and safe cardinality.

Swarm Scheduler Exporter is designed to be lightweight. Measured side by side against 1.3.2 (the last Go release) on one single-node Swarm with `--containers`, both exporting the same 964 `swarm_*` series:
| 1.x (Go) | 2.x (Rust)
Binary, linux/amd64 | 11.2 MB | 4.4 MB
Binary, linux/arm64 | 10.5 MB | 3.9 MB
Image (linux/amd64) | 13.1 MB | 6.3 MB
Idle RSS after 10 minutes | 20.1-20.6 MB | 18.6-20.4 MB

The idle RSS was read from `VmRSS` on a 32-CPU host. The Rust exporter starts one runtime worker thread per available CPU, so a host with fewer CPUs, or a CPU limit, means fewer threads and less memory: under `--cpus 2` the same exporter idled at 15.3 MB. Exact usage depends on the platform and the container runtime settings.
Docker Engine **19.03+** (Engine API **1.40**) in Swarm mode; tested on Docker **29.x**.
The exporter negotiates the API version with the daemon (`GET /version`). If `DOCKER_API_VERSION` is set, it must be within **1.40–1.56**; otherwise the exporter exits at startup with an error.

Only the latest release gets security fixes. A fix ships as a new version: released tags and image tags are immutable, so an existing version is never rebuilt or replaced. Upgrade to the latest release, or follow `ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:latest` or the `:<major>` tag.

Report it privately through GitHub's [private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/security/advisories/new), not in a public issue, a pull request or a discussion. Include the version or image digest, how the exporter is deployed (socket mount, socket proxy, TCP/TLS), and the steps or input that trigger the problem.

This is a project maintained in spare time, so reports are handled on a best-effort basis. You will get an answer in the advisory, and the fix, once released, is credited there unless you prefer otherwise.
In scope: the exporter binary, the container image published to GHCR, the release artifacts, and the workflows that build and publish them.

Out of scope: vulnerabilities in Docker or Swarm themselves, and in the base images, which are reported upstream. A base image or dependency vulnerability that affects a published release is still worth reporting here if the weekly scheduled scan has not caught it.

**Read-only by code, not by mount.** The exporter only issues read requests to the Docker API (list, inspect and events), and the code enforces that: every Docker call goes through an interface that exposes nothing else. Mounting the socket with `:ro` does not make the API read-only, and access to the Docker socket is equivalent to root on the host. To enforce read-only access at runtime, put a socket proxy in front of the Docker API: the tested example in [Behind a socket proxy](docs/deployment.md#behind-a-socket-proxy-recommended) makes the API read-only, not least-privilege: its sections match by path prefix, so the `SERVICES` and `TASKS` the exporter needs also allow service and task logs, and `CONTAINERS=1` allows every `GET` under `/containers`. See also [Security & Permissions](README.md#-security--permissions).

**Unauthenticated endpoints.** `/metrics` and `/healthz` have no authentication and are meant for an internal scrape network. Neither takes input that turns into work: no request parameter causes a Docker call.

**Supply chain.** Every GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA and every image the workflows and the Dockerfile use to an index digest. Each release image is scanned for `HIGH` and `CRITICAL` vulnerabilities before its version is tagged, and the latest release is scanned again every week, together with the Rust dependencies (cargo-deny). The release process is described in [docs/release.md](docs/release.md).
Release images carry a build provenance attestation and a keyless cosign signature from the release workflow. Verify an image by digest before you trust it:

IMAGE=ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter
DIGEST=sha256:...   # from `docker buildx imagetools inspect $IMAGE:<version>`

gh attestation verify "oci://$IMAGE@$DIGEST" --repo leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter \
  --signer-workflow leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml --source-ref refs/heads/master

cosign verify "$IMAGE@$DIGEST" \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml@refs/heads/master \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
The signature is stored as a Sigstore bundle in an OCI 1.1 referring artifact, so `cosign verify` needs cosign v3, or v2.6 or later with `--new-bundle-format`.

Prometheus Alert rule:

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Swarm service not at desired replicas (and not just updating)
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
- alert: SwarmServiceNotAtDesired
  expr: |
    (swarm_service_at_desired == 0)
    and on (stack, service)
    (swarm_service_update_state_info{state="updating"} == 0)
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: warning
    service: swarm
  annotations:
    summary: "Service {{ $labels.stack }}/{{ $labels.service }} not at desired replicas"
    description: |
      The Swarm service {{ $labels.stack }}/{{ $labels.service }} is not running
      at its desired replica count for more than 5 minutes and is not in
      an 'updating' state.
      Check the service tasks, node availability, and recent changes.

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Swarm service in rollback state
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
- alert: SwarmServiceRollbackOngoing
  expr: |
    sum by (stack, service, display_name) (
      swarm_service_update_state_info{state=~"rollback_(started|completed)"}
    ) > 0
  for: 1m
  labels:
    severity: warning
    service: swarm
  annotations:
    summary: "Service rollback detected for {{ $labels.display_name }}"
    description: |
      The Swarm service {{ $labels.display_name }} is in a rollback state
      (rollback_started or rollback_completed).
      Investigate the deployment history and task failures.

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Containers in an unhealthy / failed state (Compose/standalone)
#   - Includes: unhealthy, exited, dead
#   - Excludes: one-shot containers that exited/dead with exit_code=0
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
- alert: ContainerUnhealthy
  expr: |
    (
      sum by (display_name, stack, service) (
        swarm_container_state{
          orchestrator=~"compose|none",
          state=~"unhealthy|exited|dead"
        }
      ) > 0
    )
    UNLESS
