The exporter's command-line flags, the Docker client's environment variables and the limits on custom labels.

Usage: swarm-scheduler-exporter [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --listen-addr <string>
          IP address and port to bind [default: 0.0.0.0:8888]
      --poll-delay <duration>
          How often to poll tasks (e.g. 10s, 1m, 1m30s). Minimum 1s. [default: 10s]
      --containers[=<BOOL>]
          Expose container state metrics (opt-in).
      --containers-include-swarm[=<BOOL>]
          Include containers belonging to Swarm tasks.
      --log-format <string>
          Either json or text [default: text] [possible values: text, json]
      --log-level <string>
          Either debug, info, warn, error [default: info] [possible values: debug, info, warn, error]
      --log-time[=<BOOL>]
          Include timestamp in logs
      --healthcheck[=<BOOL>]
          Probe this exporter's /healthz on --listen-addr and exit 0 if healthy, 1 otherwise
      --label <value>
          Name of custom service labels to add to metrics
  -h, --help
          Display help message
Flags are long options with two dashes only. A single-dash spelling (`-poll-delay`) is refused with a pointer to the `--` one, and so is any positional argument (exit code `2`).
A value goes after a space or `=` (`--poll-delay 30s`, `--poll-delay=30s`); a repeated flag keeps its last value, and `--label` may be repeated (an empty name is refused).
A boolean flag alone means `true`; turning one off takes `=` (`--containers=false`; only `true` and `false` are accepted). `--containers false` is refused: `false` would be a positional argument.

`--log-level` takes `debug`, `info`, `warn` (also `warning`) or `error`, and `--log-format` takes `json` or `text`, in any case; anything else is refused at startup (exit code `2`). Logs go to standard output, the timestamps (`--log-time`) are UTC RFC 3339, and a line carries its fields as `key=value` (text) or as JSON members (json).
`--poll-delay` takes a duration (`500ms`, `10s`, `1m30s`, `1m 30s`) of at least `1s` (exit code `1` otherwise). A bool flag takes `true` or `false` (`--containers`, `--containers=true`).
`-h` and `--help` print the help to standard output and exit `0`.
`DOCKER_HOST` — Docker daemon URL
`DOCKER_CERT_PATH` — Path to TLS certs
`DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY` — Enable TLS verification (set to `1`)
`DOCKER_API_VERSION` — Pin the Engine API version instead of negotiating it (`<major>.<minor>`, within 1.40–1.56)
The client connects to `DOCKER_HOST` directly: `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY` are not read. To go through a proxy (a socket proxy, say), point `DOCKER_HOST` at it.

Names are validated & **sanitized** to Prometheus label rules: ASCII `[a-zA-Z0-9_]` only, every other character (non-ASCII letters included) becomes `_`, and a name that would start with a digit gets a leading `_` (e.g., `app.kubernetes.io/name` → `app_kubernetes_io_name`, `équipe` → `_quipe`). Label values are kept as they are.

⚠️ Earlier versions kept non-ASCII letters in label names. If a `--label` name has one, its series label name changes (`tëam` is now `t_am`): update the queries, dashboards and alerts that use it. A name that starts with two or more non-ASCII characters (`команда`, `团队`, `ÜÖteam`) now sanitizes to a name starting with `__`, which is reserved: the exporter rejects it at startup, and the `--label` must be renamed.
Duplicate/colliding sanitized names are rejected at startup, and so is a sanitized name starting with `__` (reserved by Prometheus).
At most **8** custom label keys; more are rejected at startup.
A name that sanitizes to a label the exporter already uses (`stack`, `service`, `service_mode`, `display_name`, `state`) is rejected at startup.
Suspicious **high-cardinality values** log a one-time warning.
When running the exporter inside a container, it needs permission to talk to the Docker Engine. On most systems, this means allowing access to the Docker UNIX socket at `/var/run/docker.sock`.
Docker’s socket is owned by a specific group (e.g., `docker` or `root`). Check the numeric group ID (GID) on your system:
stat -c %g /var/run/docker.sock
Use that GID in the `--group` or `--group-add` flag so the container’s user (the image sets an explicit non-root `USER 65532:65532`) can connect to the socket.
If you skip this step, you’ll see errors like:
permission denied while trying to connect to the Docker daemon socket
⚠️ The GID must be the same on **all Swarm manager nodes** if you use a bind mount for the socket. If GIDs differ, use the **TCP/TLS approach** below instead of the socket.

docker run --rm \
 -p 8888:8888 \
 -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro \
 --group-add 140 \
 ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:latest \
 --log-format text \
 --log-level warn
Replace `140` with the value from `stat -c %g /var/run/docker.sock`.

docker service create \
 --name swarm-scheduler-exporter \
 --mode replicated --replicas 1 \
 --constraint 'node.role == manager' \
 --group 140 \
 --mount type=bind,src=/var/run/docker.sock,dst=/var/run/docker.sock \
 --read-only \
 --mount type=tmpfs,dst=/tmp,tmpfs-size=16m \
 --publish published=8888,target=8888 \
 ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:latest \
 --poll-delay 10s
ℹ️ **Why the `manager` constraint?** Only manager nodes can access cluster-wide service, node, and event data required by the exporter.

The exporter only reads, but whatever holds the Docker socket can do anything. Put [tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy](https://github.com/Tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy) in front of it: the exporter then reaches the Docker API over an internal overlay network, and the proxy refuses every write and every API section the allowlist leaves off. A ready Swarm stack is in [`deployments/docker/docker-compose.socket-proxy.yaml`](../deployments/docker/docker-compose.socket-proxy.yaml), with the allowlist in [`deployments/docker/socket-proxy.env`](../deployments/docker/socket-proxy.env):

cd deployments/docker
docker stack deploy -c docker-compose.socket-proxy.yaml monitoring

The allowlist sets every ACL variable of the pinned proxy image explicitly (the image enables `EVENTS` and `VERSION` by default) and opens only `VERSION`, `EVENTS`, `SERVICES`, `NODES`, `TASKS` and `CONTAINERS`. `TestSocketProxy_ExampleAllowlist` runs the pinned image with that file against a real Swarm, and checks that the exporter works through it and that what is left off is refused.

⚠️ **Scope:** this makes the Docker API **read-only** for the exporter, not least-privilege. The proxy matches each section by path prefix, so every enabled section allows every `GET` under it, and logs, specs and container files can hold secrets: - `SERVICES=1` and `TASKS=1`, which the exporter always needs, also allow service and task logs (`/services/<id>/logs`, `/tasks/<id>/logs`: the containers' logs, from across the Swarm), and the service list the exporter reads carries every service spec, environment variables included. - `CONTAINERS=1` allows every `GET` under `/containers`, including logs, stats, `top`, `archive` and `export`. `CONTAINERS` is needed only with `--containers`: without that flag, set it to `0`. That narrows the exposure, but log access stays. Exact per-endpoint rules would need a custom `haproxy.cfg`, which the example does not attempt.
Two proxy behaviours to know:

HAProxy cuts an idle event stream after its client timeout (about 10 minutes; a quiet stream was held 660s). It ends the stream without the chunked body's terminating chunk, so the exporter logs `event stream ended; will reconnect` at warn, then reconnects (and resyncs). A server timeout, a proxy restart and a stopped daemon end the stream the same way.
The task poll sends no filter in its URL, so a large cluster never runs into HAProxy's request size limit.
If your nodes have mismatched socket GIDs or you prefer not to expose `/var/run/docker.sock`, you can use Docker’s authenticated API instead:

docker service create \
 --name swarm-scheduler-exporter \
 --mode replicated --replicas 1 \
 --constraint 'node.role == manager' \
 --read-only \
 --mount type=tmpfs,dst=/tmp,tmpfs-size=16m \
 --publish published=8888,target=8888 \
 --env DOCKER_HOST=tcp://manager.example.internal:2376 \
 --env DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1 \
 --mount type=bind,src=/path/to/certs,dst=/run/certs,ro \
 --env DOCKER_CERT_PATH=/run/certs \
 ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:latest \
 --poll-delay 10s
This avoids group and permission issues, relying instead on proper TLS authentication.

A complete Compose setup (replicated mode, manager constraint, and environment hints) is available at: [`deployments/docker/docker-compose.yaml`](../deployments/docker/docker-compose.yaml). The socket-proxy stack is in [`deployments/docker/docker-compose.socket-proxy.yaml`](../deployments/docker/docker-compose.socket-proxy.yaml).
All metrics live under the `swarm_` namespace.
Every service-level metric, including the update/rollback metrics below, carries these service identity labels. All except `swarm_service_restart_policy` also carry custom labels:
`stack` — the stack namespace (`com.docker.stack.namespace`), empty for a service not deployed as part of a stack
`service` — the service name without the `<stack>_` prefix
`service_mode` — `replicated`, `global`, `replicated-job` or `global-job`, as in the `MODE` column of `docker service ls`
`display_name` — `stack service`, or just the stack (or service) name when the two are equal or the stack is empty
one label per `--label` flag (see [Custom label guardrails](configuration.md#custom-label-guardrails)), with the value of that service label, empty when the service does not set it
`...custom` below stands for those custom labels.

`swarm_service_desired_replicas{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom}` Desired replicas (**replicated**: configured replicas; **global**: number of eligible nodes, e.g. `6` on a healthy 6-node cluster with no constraints; **replicated-job**: the job's total completions; **global-job**: number of eligible nodes). A node is eligible when it is `ready` + `active` and meets the service's placement constraints and platforms. Placement-constraint evaluation follows Swarm: values are case-insensitive, a missing label compares as empty, and `node.ip` supports an IP or CIDR.

`swarm_task_replicas_state{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,state,...custom}` Task count by state, counting the **current task per slot** for replicated services and replicated jobs or **per node** for global services and global jobs (always emits zeros for all known states per current service). Jobs count only the tasks of their **current iteration**: tasks left behind by an earlier run of the job are skipped.

`swarm_service_running_replicas{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom}` Number of **currently running** tasks per service (current task per slot or node, same snapshot as `replicas_state`). A service with no tasks at all (e.g. one never scheduled anywhere) still gets `0` here and in `replicas_state`, plus an `at_desired` series, so an alert on `at_desired == 0` also covers a service whose tasks were never created.

ℹ️ **Current task:** the task Swarm still wants (desired state not `shutdown`, `remove`, …), preferring a running one, then the newest. A task Swarm has retired that has not reported stopping is not counted in any family: a down node keeps showing its tasks' last state (for example `running`) for up to 24h, and a live node takes a moment to report a task it is stopping. A retired task that did stop (for example `failed` after its restarts ran out) still counts under its state. This is why `running_replicas` can differ from the `REPLICAS` column of `docker service ls` during node outages and updates. ℹ️ **Consistency:** each poll counts tasks against one snapshot of the exporter's service and node caches, and a service's counts are published only if nothing about it changed while its tasks were listed: not its spec (replica count, mode, placement, job iteration), not a pending event for it, not the node list for a global service or global job, and no resync was requested. A rejected service keeps its previously published `replicas_state`, `running_replicas` and `at_desired` series for up to **2** polls in a row (only if its labels did not change); on the 3rd rejection in a row its series are dropped and the poll counts as failed, so health turns red instead of the exporter publishing stale numbers. Rejections are counted in `swarm_exporter_poll_rejections_total`.

`swarm_service_at_desired{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom}` `1` if `running_replicas == desired_replicas`, else `0`. Useful for dead-simple SLOs and alerting. **Jobs** are at desired once they have **finished**: every task of the current iteration that Swarm still wants is `complete`, and there are at least `desired_replicas` of them for a replicated job. For a global job, every node that is eligible **now** must have a completed task of the current iteration, so a node that becomes eligible after the job ran keeps it at `0` until its own task completes. While a job is still running, `at_desired` is `0`.

`swarm_service_schedulable_replicas{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom}` Number of replicas that can currently be scheduled given node availability and placement constraints. **Replicated**: `min(configured_replicas, eligible_nodes)` — drops to `0` when the only eligible node for a constrained service is offline. **Global**: equal to `desired_replicas` (eligible-node count). **One-shot / cronjob services** (`RestartPolicy.Condition == "none"`): always `0`, since the scheduler is not expected to keep tasks running for them. This silences false positives for swarm-cronjob–managed services that idle at `running=0` between runs. **Jobs** (`replicated-job`, `global-job`): always `0` too, since a job's tasks run to completion and exit. Architecture matching for `Placement.Platforms` normalizes kernel-style names (`x86_64`, `aarch64`, `armv7l`, `i686`, …) to Docker manifest names ( `amd64`, `arm64`, `arm`, `386`, …) on both sides of the comparison, so a manager that reports `x86_64` correctly matches a service requiring `amd64`. Prefer this over `desired_replicas` in alert expressions to suppress false positives when a pinned node is down:
swarm_service_running_replicas < on(stack,service,service_mode,display_name) swarm_service_schedulable_replicas

`swarm_service_restart_policy{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,restart_condition}` Exhaustive `0`/`1` gauges for `none`, `on-failure` and `any`. A missing policy or empty condition defaults to `any`. Unlike `schedulable_replicas=0`, the policy identifies intentionally one-shot services, but does not prove successful completion. This family carries **no custom labels**, so `restart_condition` remains usable as a custom label on existing families. Join using `on(stack,service,service_mode,display_name)`, for example:
swarm_service_running_replicas and on(stack,service,service_mode,display_name) (swarm_service_restart_policy{restart_condition="none"} == 1)

ℹ️ **Global services:** `desired_replicas` is the number of eligible nodes, not `0`. It is `0` only when no node is eligible: none is `ready` + `active` (a node that is down, disconnected, paused, or drained does not count), or none meets the placement constraints or platforms. `running_replicas` is then usually `0` too, and `at_desired=1` only when it is. A paused or disconnected node can still run an existing task, which gives `running_replicas > desired_replicas` ⇒ `at_desired=0`. Tasks Swarm has retired on a down node are not counted, even while the node still reports them running; until Swarm retires them (shortly after the node goes down) they still count.

`swarm_service_update_state_info{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom,state}` = `1` for the *current* state, else `0`. States: `updating`, `completed`, `paused`, `rollback_started`, `rollback_completed`.
`swarm_service_update_started_timestamp_seconds{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom}`
`swarm_service_update_completed_timestamp_seconds{stack,service,service_mode,display_name,...custom}`
`swarm_cluster_nodes_by_state{role,availability,status}` Count of nodes by manager/worker, active/pause/drain, and ready/down/… .
`swarm_node_info{node_id,node,role}` — identity, value `1`; role is the Docker wire text.
`swarm_node_status{node_id,node,status}` — exhaustive `0`/`1` gauges for `ready`, `down`, `disconnected`, `unknown`.
`swarm_node_availability{node_id,node,availability}` — exhaustive `0`/`1` gauges for `active`, `pause`, `drain`. An empty availability emits all zeros.
`swarm_node_manager_reachability{node_id,node,reachability}` — managers only, exhaustive `0`/`1` gauges for `reachable`, `unreachable`, `unknown`.
`swarm_node_manager_leader{node_id,node}` — managers only, `1` for the leader, otherwise `0`. A missing `Leader` is `0`; workers have no manager series.

`node` is `Description.Hostname`; `node_id` distinguishes nodes with duplicate hostnames (including nodes that left and rejoined). All five families are published in one snapshot; removed nodes and old role identities disappear. Node and manager status is normally refreshed about every minute; node events refresh sooner, and failures can delay updates. The full resync still runs every 5 minutes. Missing status or reachability maps to `unknown`. Unknown enum values invented by a newer daemon fail the Docker call during decoding, rather than passing through as labels (see [Q16](migration.md#coming-from-1x-go)).
`swarm_exporter_health` — `1` healthy / `0` unhealthy.
`swarm_exporter_build_info{version,commit,date}` — `1`.
`swarm_exporter_polls_total` / `swarm_exporter_poll_errors_total`.
`swarm_exporter_poll_duration_seconds` (histogram).
`swarm_exporter_events_reconnects_total`.
`swarm_exporter_events_dropped_total` — Swarm events ignored because they carried no actor ID.
`swarm_exporter_poll_rejections_total` — per-service poll counts not published because the service changed while its tasks were listed (see **Consistency** above).

`swarm_exporter_resyncs_total{result}` — resyncs (service and node list) by `result`: `success` or `failure`. Both series exist at `0` from startup, so `increase()` and "never failed" rules work before the first resync. A resync interrupted by shutdown is not counted.
`swarm_exporter_last_poll_success_timestamp_seconds` — Unix time of the latest successfully published task poll; `0` until the first one.
`swarm_exporter_last_resync_success_timestamp_seconds` — Unix time of the latest completed resync; `0` until the first one.
For example:

- alert: SwarmExporterResyncsFailing
  expr: increase(swarm_exporter_resyncs_total{result="failure"}[30m]) > 3
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Swarm exporter resyncs keep failing"

- alert: SwarmExporterPollsStale
  expr: time() - swarm_exporter_last_poll_success_timestamp_seconds > 120
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "Swarm exporter has not published a task poll for over 2 minutes"
Beside the `swarm_*` families, `/metrics` carries the process metrics the Prometheus Go client exports by default, with the same names, types and help texts:

`process_cpu_seconds_total`, `process_open_fds`, `process_max_fds`, `process_virtual_memory_bytes`, `process_virtual_memory_max_bytes`, `process_resident_memory_bytes`, `process_start_time_seconds`, `process_network_receive_bytes_total` and `process_network_transmit_bytes_total` (Linux).
There are no `go_*` metrics (the exporter has no Go runtime) and no `promhttp_metric_handler_*` ones (the scrape handler is not promhttp).

The exposition is always OpenMetrics text (`application/openmetrics-text; version=1.0.0; charset=utf-8`), uncompressed and ending with `# EOF`, whatever the scraper's `Accept` and `Accept-Encoding`. Prometheus reads it without a setting. In it a counter's family is named without `_total` (`# TYPE swarm_exporter_polls counter`), and its sample carries it (`swarm_exporter_polls_total`): the metric names a query uses are the same.
If you also run non-Swarm workloads (e.g. plain Docker Compose or standalone containers), the exporter can expose **container state** metrics when started with `--containers`.

`swarm_container_state{project,stack,service,container,orchestrator,display_name,state,exit_code}` Emits an **info-style one-hot series** per container across all known states. Exactly one time series per container has `1`, the rest are `0`.
`project` / `service` — from Compose labels (`com.docker.compose.*`), if present
`stack` — from Swarm labels (`com.docker.stack.namespace`), if present
`container` — the container's first name without its leading `/`, as Docker reports it (not sanitized)
`orchestrator` — `compose`, `swarm`, or `none`
`display_name` — friendly name (`stack service` or `stack` if identical)
`state` — one of `created`, `restarting`, `running`, `removing`, `paused`, `exited`, `dead`, `healthy`, `unhealthy`, `health_starting`
`exit_code` — string exit code (only when `state="exited"`, otherwise empty)

ℹ️ The container list does not say which containers have a healthcheck, so the exporter inspects **every running container** (to read its health state, if any) and **every exited container** (to read its exit code). Inspects are capped at **300 per poll**, failed ones included, and share one **10s** deadline per poll; a container past the cap or the deadline keeps its listed state and an empty `exit_code`. Swarm task containers are skipped unless `--containers-include-swarm` is set.

This page covers the two jumps: **2.x to 3.0** (the Rust exporter moves onto shared, standard libraries and stops reproducing Go's behaviour byte for byte) and, below it, **1.x (Go) to Rust**. Either way every `swarm_*` metric keeps its name, type, help text, labels and values, `/metrics` and `/healthz` keep their paths, and the Docker access stays read-only. The metric names, types and label names are pinned by a committed inventory taken from the 1.3.2 exposition (minus the `go_*` and `promhttp_*` families), and the values the Docker fixtures feed are checked by tests.
Before you roll it out:

**Scrape config and dashboards.** `/metrics` is OpenMetrics text only (`Content-Type: application/openmetrics-text; version=1.0.0; charset=utf-8`), never compressed, and ends with `# EOF`. Prometheus 2.5+ and 3.x negotiate it; a custom scraper that needs text 0.0.4 or protobuf does not work. A counter's *family* has no `_total` (its sample has), the `promhttp_*` families and `?name[]=` filtering are gone, and `process_*` is unchanged. Queries on sample names need no change.

**Docker socket proxy.** The client negotiates the API version with `GET /version`, not `/_ping`: set `VERSION=1` (and `PING=0`, which is no longer used) in your proxy's allowlist, or pin `DOCKER_API_VERSION` (`<major>.<minor>`, within 1.40 to 1.56). Without either the exporter logs that the negotiation was refused and sends requests with no version prefix. The example in `deployments/docker/socket-proxy.env` is updated.

**Log parsers.** Logs are `tracing` lines: text (`level`, `message`, then `key=value` fields) or JSON (`level`, `message`, the fields, `target`), timestamps in UTC (`TZ` has no effect), the error field is `error` (it was `err`), and durations print as `500ms`, `1m 30s`. `--log-format plain` and `--log-level fatal|panic` are refused (exit 2); `warning` is still an alias of `warn`.

**Flag values.** A bool flag takes `true` or `false` only: `--containers=1`, `=t`, `=TRUE`, `=0` and the other `strconv.ParseBool` spellings are refused (exit 2). `--poll-delay` takes `10s`, `500ms`, `1m30s`, `1m 30s`, `1.5s` (and `2d`), no sign: `-5s` is a parse error (exit 2), not the exit-1 minimum check; the minimum is still `1s`.
**Placement constraints** (`node.ip` with a CIDR such as `10.0.0.0/024` written with a leading-zero prefix, constraint keys and values with non-ASCII letters) read slightly differently, see Q17.

**Docker states.** A task, node, container or event value the Docker API documents is read as before; one a *newer daemon invents* fails the call that carries it (logged by the collector), where 2.x passed it on as text.

**HTTP edge cases.** Any other path is a bodyless 404, a method other than GET or HEAD is 405, and a listen error reads `http listen: listen tcp <address>: <system error>` (Q13). The listener is dual-stack on `:port`.
The rows that changed since 2.x are Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q6, Q11, Q13, Q15, Q16 and Q17 in the table below.
2.0 is the same exporter rewritten in Rust; the flags' names and defaults, the health rules and the Docker access are unchanged, and the wire format is the one thing that moved (Q2).
What to change when upgrading from 1.x, besides the 3.0 list above:

**Flags take two dashes.** `-poll-delay 10s` becomes `--poll-delay 10s`, `-containers` becomes `--containers`, and so on, in `command:`, `docker run` and `docker service create` arguments. 1.x accepted both spellings; the exporter refuses the single-dash one at startup and names the `--` one.

**Healthchecks you override** run `--healthcheck`: `test: [ "CMD", "/usr/local/bin/swarm-scheduler-exporter", "--healthcheck" ]`. The image's own `HEALTHCHECK` and the compose examples in `deployments/docker/` already do.
**Dashboards or alerts on `go_*` metrics** have nothing to read: use `process_*` instead.
**`DOCKER_CERT_PATH` without `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY`** no longer connects without verifying the daemon's certificate: set `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1`.

**A TCP `DOCKER_HOST` reached through `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY`** is now dialled directly. If the daemon is reachable only through that proxy, point `DOCKER_HOST` at a proxy that forwards to it (a socket proxy). A unix socket was never proxied.
Every intended difference, 1.x (Go) against this release (the rows above that changed since 2.x read as written here):
Q1 | Runtime metrics | `go_*`, `process_*` and `promhttp_metric_handler_*` | No `go_*` and no `promhttp_metric_handler_*`; `process_*` keeps the same Linux families, names, types and help texts

Q2 | `/metrics` formats | Negotiated from `Accept`: protobuf (delimited, text, compact) or text 0.0.4; gzip by `Accept-Encoding` | Always OpenMetrics text (`application/openmetrics-text; version=1.0.0; charset=utf-8`), never compressed; a counter's family has no `_total` (its sample has); `?name[]=` filtering is gone

Q3 | CLI | Go's `flag`: `-x` and `--x` both work, trailing positional arguments are ignored (`-containers false` meant `true`), `-h` printed usage to standard error | `--x` only; a single-dash flag and any positional argument are refused (exit 2); `-h`/`--help` print to standard output and exit 0. Kept: names, defaults, last value wins, `--containers=false`, repeatable `--label`, exit 2 on parse errors. See Q17 for the value spellings

Q4 | Log flags | An unknown `-log-level` or `-log-format` silently fell back to `info` / `text` | Refused (exit 2), the message naming the accepted values; `plain` (format) and `fatal`, `panic` (level) are no longer accepted, `warning` stays an alias of `warn`

Q5 | Docker TLS | `DOCKER_CERT_PATH` with an empty `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY` meant TLS without verifying the daemon | Startup fails (`docker client init failed`, exit 1) and asks for `DOCKER_TLS_VERIFY=1`; trust roots stay the system pool plus `ca.pem`

Q6 | Events connect | `event stream connected` was logged, and a reconnect's resync requested, even when the connect failed | Both happen only once the engine has answered the events request's headers with a 2xx, however quiet the stream is after: a refused request (non-2xx, no connection) or headers that do not arrive within 15s (the request timeout) is a failed connect and goes straight to the warn path
Q7 | Reconnect backoff | The 500ms backoff reset only after a stream that carried an event, so a quiet cluster behind a proxy backed off to 30s | It resets after any stream that connected
Q8 | Shutdown | 10s for the HTTP drain, then an unbounded wait for the workers | One 10s budget from the signal to exit, covering the drain and the workers
Q9 | Error texts | Library errors in Go's and the Docker SDK's wording | Library errors in Rust's and bollard's wording; every prefix and message the exporter writes itself is unchanged
Q10 | Panic recovery | `reconciler recovered from panic` with a Go stack trace | The same record, with the panic message and a Rust backtrace

Q11 | Docker wire | User-Agent `moby-client/…`; one version ping per concurrent first request | User-Agent `swarm-scheduler-exporter/<version>`; the version is negotiated once with `GET /version` (a refusal, as a socket proxy with `VERSION=0` gives, is logged and requests then carry no version prefix; set `VERSION=1` in the proxy or pin `DOCKER_API_VERSION`)
Q12 | Go runtime environment | `GOMAXPROCS`, `GOMEMLIMIT`, `GOGC` and `GODEBUG` tuned the process | No effect; the worker count follows the CPUs available to the container

Q13 | HTTP edge cases | net/http's answers to malformed requests, its header-count and size limits, the 307 for unclean paths, any method on the two routes, four server timeouts (read header 5s, read 10s, write 15s, idle 60s), and `net.Listen`'s wording and service-name ports (`:http`) | axum and hyper's: a bodyless 404 for any other path, 405 for a method other than GET and HEAD, hyper's answers and limits (431 above 100 headers), no redirect for unclean paths; a 5s header-read timeout that also closes an idle keep-alive connection, and a 15s write-stall timeout (no read or idle timeout); a listen error reads `http listen: listen tcp <address>: <system error>`, a port is a number, and a host name binds its first IPv4 address. Paths, status codes and bodies of `/metrics` and `/healthz` are unchanged

Q14 | Docker proxy variables | A TCP `DOCKER_HOST` went through `HTTP_PROXY` / `HTTPS_PROXY` (honouring `NO_PROXY` and skipping loopback), as Go's `http.ProxyFromEnvironment` decides | The client dials `DOCKER_HOST` directly and reads no proxy variable; unix sockets are unaffected

Q15 | Log output | slog text/JSON/plain lines, timestamps in the local zone (`TZ`) | `tracing` text or JSON lines (`level`, `message`, then the fields; JSON adds `target`), timestamps in UTC; the fields keep their names except `err`, now `error`, and durations print as Rust writes them (`500ms`, `1s`)

Q16 | Docker client | moby client v0.6.0 over its own HTTP/1 transport; every state a string; `DOCKER_API_VERSION` within 1.40–1.56 | bollard through `docker-client`: a state or type the daemon documents is decoded, one a newer daemon invents fails the call that carries it (a decode error, logged by the collector); requests carry the `/v<major>.<minor>` prefix of the pinned or negotiated version (none before negotiation, or after a refused one); the container list asks `all=true&size=false`; a pin must be `<major>.<minor>` within 1.40–1.56

Q17 | Value spellings | Bool flags took every `strconv.ParseBool` spelling (`1`, `t`, `T`, `TRUE`, `True`, `0`, `f`, `F`, `FALSE`, `False`); `--poll-delay` took Go durations, a leading sign included; a `node.ip` CIDR took a prefix length with leading zeros (`10.0.0.0/024`); constraints and container labels folded case by Go's simple folding; custom-label errors quoted values with `%q` | Bool flags take `true` or `false` only (exit 2 otherwise); `--poll-delay` takes humantime durations (`10s`, `500ms`, `1m30s`, `1m 30s`, `1.5s`, `5µs`, and now `2d`), but no sign: `-5s` is a parse error (exit 2, where Go's reached the exit-1 minimum check), and a bare number needs a unit as before; a CIDR prefix has no leading zeros (the constraint never matches); constraint keys and values compare by Unicode lowercase, so U+017F (long s) no longer equals `s`; custom-label errors quote with `{:?}`; a poll delay prints as `10s`, `1h 2m`, `1s 500ms`
**Data races**: one reconciler task owns every cache and per-service metric write; removed the shared global node count; no per-event tasks.
**Event resiliency**: reconnect with capped backoff and a resync on every reconnect; a bounded dirty set that falls back to a full resync; periodic resync.

**Series lifecycle**: `replicas_state` is rebuilt and published as one snapshot per poll, so a scrape never sees it empty or partial; exhaustive zero emission per current service; delete series on service remove.
**Global desired replicas accuracy**: evaluate **eligible nodes** (status/availability/constraints/platforms), not total nodes.
**Label sanitation & validation**: full Prometheus regex, collision checks, max label keys, high-cardinality warning, raw→sanitized mapping.
**Operability**: graceful shutdown; `/healthz`; health/build/exporter metrics; quieter default logs; validated `--poll-delay`.

**Performance**: node snapshot cache; on node events recompute every service from cached placement, without inspecting it; task poll optimized to “current task per slot/node”; burst events coalesced per service.
**Metrics namespace**: consistent `swarm_*` names & labels aligned with Prometheus best practices.
**Service update visibility**: `swarm_service_update_state_info` + timestamps for rollbacks/paused/update flows.
**SLO helpers**: `swarm_service_running_replicas` and `swarm_service_at_desired` for direct alerting/dashboards.

**Footprint**: since 2.0 a static Rust binary on a distroless base, with a smaller image and binary than the Go 1.x releases (see [Resource usage](../README.md#-resource-usage)), and a Docker client that can only send read requests.
How the exporter reports its health and how it follows the Docker event stream.

The exporter is healthy once its first resync (service and node list) has completed, a task poll has been published, and the latest published poll is no older than `max(3 × --poll-delay, 30s)` (30s with the default 10s poll delay). A requested resync that stays outstanding for longer than that same window, for example because listing services keeps failing, makes it unhealthy too.

HTTP: `/healthz` responds `200` with body `ok` when healthy, and `503` with a short reason (`initial resync not completed`, `no successful poll yet`, `last poll too old` or `resync outstanding`) when not.
Metric: `swarm_exporter_health` reports the same check as `1` healthy / `0` unhealthy, evaluated at every scrape.

Container health: the image is distroless (no shell, no curl), so it ships a `HEALTHCHECK` that runs the binary itself with `--healthcheck`. That mode requests `/healthz` on `--listen-addr` (a wildcard host such as `0.0.0.0` or `::` is probed on loopback), never through a proxy and without following redirects, and exits `0` on a `200` and `1` otherwise, printing the status and the reason. The check allows a 90s start period for the first resync, then probes every 30s; after 3 failures the container is unhealthy and Swarm replaces the task, which is the intended remedy for a stuck exporter.
The image's check uses the default `--listen-addr`. If you change it, override the check with the same address:

services:
  exporter:
    command: [ "--listen-addr", "0.0.0.0:9100" ]
    healthcheck:
      test: [ "CMD", "/usr/local/bin/swarm-scheduler-exporter", "--healthcheck", "--listen-addr", "0.0.0.0:9100" ]
To turn it off, set `healthcheck: disable: true` in compose or a stack file, or pass `--no-healthcheck` to `docker run` or `docker service create`.

A reconnect resumes the stream from just before the last event seen; the resync covers what the daemon no longer replays, such as the events of a restart. A stream that ends cleanly is logged at info, any other stream end at warn. A socket proxy cutting an idle stream (HAProxy does so after its client timeout, about 10 minutes, on a quiet cluster) ends it without the chunked body's terminating chunk, so that is logged at warn too, followed by the reconnect. Individual event JSON records are limited to 1 MiB, excluding leading whitespace and JSON-sequence record separators. An oversized record ends the stream at warn, followed by a reconnect and resync.

How a swarm-scheduler-exporter release is versioned, built and published, what to do when one fails halfway, and what has to be set up by hand for all of it to hold. The pipeline is [`.github/workflows/release.yaml`](../.github/workflows/release.yaml), built from the shared actions of [gh-composite-actions](https://github.com/leinardi/gh-composite-actions) (`release-version`, `require-ci-green`, `release-mode`, `toolchain-record`, `toolchain-recover`, `check-pinned-bases`, `trivy-gate`, `binary-attestation-status`); this page is why it is shaped that way.

Two static binaries, `swarm-scheduler-exporter-linux-amd64` and `swarm-scheduler-exporter-linux-arm64`, cross-compiled for the `x86_64-unknown-linux-musl` and `aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` targets by `make rust-release-binaries` (`cargo zigbuild --release --locked`), with the build paths remapped and the version, commit and commit date compiled in, plus `checksums.txt` over both. All three are attached to the GitHub release, and each binary has a [build provenance attestation](https://docs.github.com/actions/security-guides/using-artifact-attestations) from the release workflow.

A multi-arch (`linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64`) image at `ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:<version>`, built from the Dockerfile's `prebuilt` target: **each platform's image binary is that platform's release binary, byte for byte**. It carries an SBOM and `mode=max` BuildKit provenance in its index, a build provenance attestation and a keyless [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/) signature made with the release workflow's own OIDC identity. Before the version was tagged, CI had passed on the commit (the full image suite on amd64 and the reduced one on arm64, [What CI proves](#what-ci-proves)), and both platform images passed the release's short smoke test and a [Trivy](https://trivy.dev/) scan with no fixable `HIGH` or `CRITICAL` vulnerability outside [`.trivyignore.yaml`](../.trivyignore.yaml).
The moving image tags `:<major>` and `:latest`, and the GitHub "Latest" release marker, when the version is the highest released one.

A GitHub release whose notes name the Rust toolchain the binaries were built with and the base digest each platform image was built on (read from the build's provenance), followed by notes generated from the merged pull requests.
Verify what was published:

gh attestation verify swarm-scheduler-exporter-linux-amd64 --repo leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter \
  --signer-workflow leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:<version> --repo leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter \
  --signer-workflow leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml
cosign verify ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:<version> \
  --certificate-identity https://github.com/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml@refs/heads/master \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
The workflow signs with cosign v3, which stores the signature as a Sigstore bundle in an OCI 1.1 referring artifact, so verifying it needs cosign v3, or v2.6 or later with `--new-bundle-format`.
Run the **Release swarm-scheduler-exporter** workflow from the Actions tab (or `gh workflow run release.yaml`) on `master`. It takes two inputs:

`version`: optional, `X.Y.Z` or `vX.Y.Z`. Left empty, the version is derived from the commits since the last release (see [Versioning](#versioning)). Give it explicitly to force a version, or to recover a failed run with a fresh dispatch (see [Recovering a failed publish](#recovering-a-failed-publish)).
`dry_run`: boolean, default `false`. See [Dry runs](#dry-runs).

Dispatch it once CI and the integration suite have run on the commit's push to `master`: the `ci-green` job waits for each run for up to 30 minutes, and fails if one did not pass ([What CI proves](#what-ci-proves)).

**One release runs at a time.** The workflow takes a `release` concurrency group with `cancel-in-progress: false`, so a second dispatch queues behind the first rather than racing it. Two runs in flight together would each check their version against the same latest tag, both pass, and then publish in whatever order they finished.

A merge of a Dependabot pull request releases the next patch on its own, with no dispatch, when everything since the last release is Dependabot's and at least one of its commits is a `fix(deps)` (a new runtime base image or a crate update). The workflow also runs on every push to `master`: its `dependabot` job calls gh-reusable-workflows' `dependabot-release` with `ecosystems: docker cargo`, which checks from the API alone that every unreleased commit is Dependabot's own (committed by GitHub) or the merge of its pull request, that the change only moves action pins and the versions of those ecosystems' files, and that CI passed on the push. Then the release runs as a dispatch would, with that patch as an explicit version. Anything else is a green no-op with a notice: a `chore(deps)` merge (actions, pre-commit, development dependencies) ships nothing, and a human commit waiting to be released leaves the release to a dispatch.

A push that merges a Dependabot pull request takes the same `release` group as a dispatch, so the two never publish at once and a lower version never moves `latest` after a higher one. Every other push runs in a group of its own and only skips the `dependabot` job. GitHub keeps one pending run per group: a Dependabot merge that arrives while a release runs and a dispatch waits replaces that dispatch, which shows as cancelled; dispatch it again.

Semantic versioning, derived from [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) by [`svu`](https://github.com/caarlos0/svu), as [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#commit-messages) describes:
`feat` is a minor;
`fix` is a patch;

`!` before the colon, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer, is a major. The project is already at `2.x`, so the `0.x` caveat of `svu` (a breaking change before `1.0.0` jumping straight to `1.0.0`) does not apply here.

Everything else (`build`, `chore`, `ci`, `docs`, `perf`, `refactor`, `revert`, `style`, `test`) bumps nothing, so a performance improvement, refactor or revert that users should receive is committed as a `fix` (or `feat`). When no commit since the last release is a `feat`, a `fix` or a breaking change, a run with no version **fails** with "nothing to bump". Dependabot's updates of production crates and of the image's base (`dhi.io/static`) are committed as `fix(deps)`, so either alone is enough for a patch release; its dev-dependency (test-only), GitHub Actions and pre-commit updates stay `chore(deps)` and bump nothing.

Whether derived or typed, the version must be **higher than every version already released**: tags here are immutable, so publishing a `v1.9.9` after `v1.10.0` would create a permanent lower tag. The only version a run may reuse is the one it is recovering, which is exactly this version already sitting on `HEAD`. A branch whose history does not contain the highest release derives from an older base and so fails that check; the failure names the out-of-history tag, and an explicit version higher than it is the way out.

The version is resolved by the `release-version` action. svu is installed (`setup-svu`, pinned with its checksum) only when no version is given, so a version typed by hand releases even while GitHub's release downloads fail. Only strict `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` tags are releases (`RELEASE_TAG_REGEX` in the workflow, `^v(0|[1-9][0-9]*)\.(0|[1-9][0-9]*)\.(0|[1-9][0-9]*)$`, the actions' default too): an explicit `01.2.3`, `1.2.3-rc.1`, `1.2.3+meta` or `v1.2.3.4` is refused. Every lookup filters the full tag list through that regex, never through a glob, so pointer tags (`latest`, `v1`), pre-releases and malformed tags can never become the current version, and `svu` is given the exact tag to count from, literally.
CI fetches only the tags on `origin`. A local `svu next` reads every local tag, so before reasoning about versions locally, drop the tags `origin` does not have:
git fetch --prune --prune-tags origin

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: Tags in this repository are immutable. The "Immutable tags" ruleset, managed in [gh-leinardi-iac](https://github.com/leinardi/gh-leinardi-iac), covers every tag except `v[0-9]`, `v[1-9][0-9]` and `latest`, blocks update, deletion and non-fast-forward, and has no bypass actors. A failed release cannot delete its tag, so everything that can fail happens before the tag exists, and everything after it can be finished by a re-run on the tagged commit.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: The run has four jobs:

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **`guard`**: refuse anything but `master`, failing rather than skipping when `github.ref` is not `refs/heads/master`; then resolve the version, as in [Versioning](#versioning), and read the stamps from the commit.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **`ci-green`**, after `guard`: `require-ci-green` on the commit. CI's run for the push of this exact commit to `master` (`.github/workflows/ci.yaml`, by file path, not by a check name any workflow could reuse) must have concluded `success`, with its `ci-result` job, and so must the integration suite's run for the same push (`.github/workflows/integration.yaml`, its `integration` job). This replaces the release-time clippy and test suite, and the full image tests ([What CI proves](#what-ci-proves)).

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **`audit`**, alongside the two: `cargo deny check` (advisories, licences, bans and sources), the one time-sensitive check of the code, since advisories are published every day. It needs nothing and nothing needs it, so it runs while the release job builds and costs the release almost no time: the release job waits for it (`require-job-success`) only right before its first step that publishes anything, and stops unless it passed.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **`release`**, which checks the Dockerfile pins (`check-pinned-bases`, as CI does), sets up the pinned Rust (on a recovery, the one the tag records, through `toolchain-recover`), and then **decides the mode** (`release-mode`) from the Git tag on the remote, the image `ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter:<version>`, the GitHub release and its assets. Only "not found" counts as absent: any other lookup error stops the run.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: A tag on this commit must be annotated, in the clone, and record the toolchain this run builds with (`Rust: 1.98.1`), as this workflow writes it. The tag is then created **locally only**, if it does not exist yet.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: A **fresh** release then runs:

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Build the binaries once**, with `make rust-release-binaries`, the make target CI builds them with. The Rust build cache is the release's own (`prefix-key: release`), written only by this workflow. `checksums.txt` is written over both (`make rust-release-checksums`).

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: Start a registry inside the job (`registry:3.1.2`, pinned by digest).

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Build the image once**, the Dockerfile's `prebuilt` target, for both platforms, with those binaries as the `dist` build context, so the image binary is the release asset. It is pushed by digest to the local registry, with the SBOM and `mode=max` provenance, every layer recompressed as gzip: the `dhi.io` base layers are zstd, and for a zstd image skopeo rewrites the index entries with a compression annotation, which the digest-preserving copy in step 9 then refuses. There is no layer cache: the target is the base plus one COPY.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Record the base the build used**: the base is pinned by tag, so each platform's provenance names the digest the tag resolved to. The build must have pulled exactly one digest of the base tag and the `# syntax=` frontend pin, and nothing else (apart from BuildKit's SBOM scanner, which generates the SBOM and is not part of the image); the digests go into the release notes and the summary, as the exact base the release shipped.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Smoke-test and scan both platform images**, each pulled back from the local registry by its own digest: `scripts/image-test.sh --tier smoke` checks that the image binary's sha256 is the release asset's, and that the container, started with no Docker socket, logs `<version> <short commit> <build date>` in its startup line and serves them as `swarm_exporter_build_info` on `/metrics` (arm64 under QEMU). The binary has no `--version`; a build that lost a build argument reports the `dev` defaults and fails here, before the tag. Then `trivy-gate` scans each one (see [The scan gate](#the-scan-gate)).

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Gate the tag.** The highest released version is read again from the remote; a fresh release that is no longer the highest fails with nothing pushed.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Check the version image is absent**, right before the tag.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **`git push origin <version>`**: the point of no return. The checkout keeps no credentials; the token reaches this one command as an HTTP header.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Copy to GHCR, untagged**: `skopeo copy --all --preserve-digests` to `ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter@<digest>`, with skopeo pinned by digest.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Check, attest, sign.** The index GHCR serves under the digest must hash to the tested digest; then it is attested and signed.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: **Tag the image** `:<version>`, after checking once more that the tag is absent.

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: The binary attestations, the release assets and the latest pointers follow, in every mode, as described under [Recovery guarantees](#recovery-guarantees).

heading_path: Why the build happens before the tag
blocks.text: Everything stamped into an artifact comes from the commit rather than from the clock: the version, a fixed seven-character commit prefix, the commit date as the build date (and the image's `created` label), and the commit time as BuildKit's `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`. The binaries are built with the pinned Rust toolchain, zig and cargo-zigbuild, `Cargo.lock` (`--locked`), and `--remap-path-prefix` for the checkout, the cargo home and the toolchain's `rust-src` (when installed, mapped back to the `/rustc/<commit>` prefix a machine without it writes), so a re-run of the same commit produces the same bytes, which is what lets a recovery check published assets by sha256. The image is not byte-reproducible: its provenance records the build itself, so two builds of the same commit have different index digests. That is why a recovery never compares a rebuilt index with a published one, and never rebuilds a published one.

The release runs no clippy, no test suite and only a short smoke test of the image. That is sound only because CI already ran them on the same inputs, and the `ci-green` job pins that to the commit being released:

**The same commit.** `require-ci-green` accepts only the `push` run of `ci.yaml` whose head is the release's own SHA, on `master`, and its `ci-result` job must have passed on the run's newest attempt.
**The code was tested on that commit.** `ci-result` needs the `rust` job (rustfmt, clippy, the tests, the docs and cargo-deny) and `pre-commit-all` (every hook on every file).

**The packaging was tested on that commit.** `ci-result` needs the `image` job, which runs on every pull request and every push, with no path filter. It builds the static binaries with `make rust-release-binaries`, the release's own make target, then the `prebuilt` image target from them for both platforms:

**linux/amd64, the full suite** (`scripts/image-test.sh --tier full`): the image is the platform's; its binary is the `dist/` binary just built, byte for byte; the container, started with no Docker socket, logs the stamps in its startup line and serves them as `swarm_exporter_build_info` on `/metrics`; the binary is a static x86-64 ELF, `0755 root:root`; the image runs as `65532:65532`, with the binary as its entrypoint, port 8888 exposed, the binary's own `--healthcheck` as its health check and the labels the stamps; and the container, hardened as `docker-compose.yaml` runs it and more (read-only root, no-new-privileges, every capability dropped), reports itself not ready on `/healthz` (HTTP 503) with no Docker daemon to reach, so its `--healthcheck` probe exits 1, stops cleanly on SIGTERM, and fails to start on an invalid flag value.
**linux/arm64, the reduced suite** under QEMU (`--tier reduced`): the same up to the image config, the container starting and serving its stamps included.

The exporter against a real Swarm is `integration.yaml`'s job, not this one: it runs the integration suite against the release-profile glibc binary on every pull request and every push to `master`, and the ruleset requires it on pull requests. `ci-result` cannot need a job of another workflow, so `ci-green` reads that push run's `integration` job separately ([Required checks](#required-checks)).

**The same build.** CI and the release build the binaries with the same make target, toolchain, zig and cargo-zigbuild (one value each, `meta/tests/toolchain.rs`), and the image from the same Dockerfile target and build context shape. The build arguments differ only in the stamps.

**The same base tag, not always the same base digest.** The `dhi.io` bases are pinned by tag, deliberately not by digest: dhi.io rebuilds its tags too often for digest pins to be worth following by hand. `check-pinned-bases` (with `tag-only-images: dhi.io`) fails CI and the release on a `dhi.io` base with no explicit tag or on `latest`, on any other image without a digest, and on any download not followed by a checksum check. So the release may build on a newer dhi.io rebuild of `dhi.io/static:<tag>` than the one CI tested. That is the accepted trade-off of pinning by tag: a rebuild of a distroless static base carries no code of ours, and what covers the base the release ships is the release's own smoke test and `trivy-gate` scan of that exact image, both before the tag. The release notes record the digest it shipped.

A pull request **from a fork** gets no `DHI_TOKEN`, and the base cannot be pulled without a login, so there the `image` job says so in a notice and tests nothing. The push to `master` after the merge runs it in full, and that run is the one the release gates on. Any other run without the secret fails the job.

What only the release can see is what changed since: a vulnerability published after CI ran (the scan and the audit run at release time for that reason), a newer rebuild of the base tag, and a broken image build, which the smoke test on the release's own build would catch before the tag.

The gate (`trivy-gate`, on both platform images) fails on a `HIGH` or `CRITICAL` vulnerability **with a fix upstream**; the findings with no fix yet are left out (`--ignore-unfixed`), since nothing in this repository can fix them. Trivy is always its latest release, never pinned, so every scan runs the newest checks; its vulnerability database is fetched at run time, which is the point of scanning at release time.

The base's findings count the same as the image's own: a fixable finding in `dhi.io/static` fails the release too. Its fix is usually dhi.io's next rebuild of the tag, which the next release picks up by itself, or a newer tag, which Dependabot proposes; until it ships, a reviewed entry in [`.trivyignore.yaml`](../.trivyignore.yaml) is the only way past the gate, scoped to the paths or purls it was found in, with a statement saying why and an expiry date Trivy enforces. When an entry expires, bump what carries the fix if it is out, otherwise extend the date with a fresh reason.
The binary is not built with `cargo auditable`, so Trivy cannot see its crates; cargo-deny, in the `audit` job and CI, is the check for them.

`dry_run: true` rehearses a fresh release: it resolves the version and decides the mode (so it stops, like a real run would, when the version is held or needs a human), then runs the CI gate, the audit and fresh steps 1 to 7 (the smoke tests and the scans included), and exercises step 9 by copying the index to a **second job-local registry** instead of GHCR, checking that the copy keeps its digest and one attestation manifest per platform. It also runs the binary attestation check, as a rehearsal, but attests nothing. It pushes no tag and publishes nothing. A dry run of a version whose image already exists stops at step 7.

The job summary shows the version, the previous tag, whether the version was explicit, the mode a real run would take, the index and platform digests, the base and the checksums; `dist/` is uploaded as the workflow artifact `dry-run-<version>-<attempt>`. A dry run with no version is also the quickest way to see what version the commits would produce.
A recovery runs on the tagged commit, because that is the only commit the tag check accepts for an existing tag:

**"Re-run all jobs" on the failed run.** This always works: a re-run keeps the original run's commit and inputs, whatever has been merged since, and that commit's CI already passed. Use "Re-run all jobs", not "Re-run failed jobs", unless `audit` itself failed: the release job accepts only an `audit` of its own attempt (`require-job-success` never trusts an earlier attempt's pass), and "Re-run failed jobs" does not re-run an `audit` that passed, so the release would wait for it until the step times out.
**A fresh dispatch with the same version, given explicitly**, while `master` still points at the tagged commit.

`release-mode` then decides **per platform**, so the image binary and the release asset of a platform never diverge. "Published" means the image (or its platform manifest) is on GHCR, or the release, draft or not, carries the asset; each must be attested by this workflow for this commit, and the image signed by it too, or the run stops.
Published for a platform | The binary comes from | What happens
Image and asset | the image | they must be the same bytes, or the run stops
Image only | the image | it is extracted, attested and uploaded as the asset
Asset only | the asset | it is downloaded and verified, and the image is built with it
Neither | a rebuild | it is built now, with the recorded toolchain

**Recovery, reuse**, when `:<version>` exists and is attested and signed by this workflow for this commit: nothing is built; missing assets are extracted from the image. The image is scanned, and findings are reported as warnings: it is already published and immutable.

**Recovery, publish**, when the tag exists and `:<version>` does not: the image is built from the published binaries where there are any and rebuilt ones for the other platform, then checked against the pins, smoke-tested, scanned, copied, checked, attested, signed and tagged. If the scan now fails, because a fixable vulnerability was published since, **the version is abandoned**: its tag stays, with no image, and the fix goes out as a higher version.

A published image that lacks a shipped platform stops the run: a manifest list cannot gain a platform without changing its digest. A tag made before the toolchain was recorded in its annotation cannot be recovered either (`toolchain-recover` and `release-mode` fail closed on it); every release since this workflow records it.

The workflow artifacts carry the run attempt in their names (`binaries-<version>-<attempt>`, `dry-run-<version>-<attempt>`), because a re-run stays inside the same workflow run and `upload-artifact` refuses to overwrite the first attempt's upload. There is no cleanup step and the tag is never deleted. If the release is wrong rather than incomplete (the wrong commit, a bad build), the answer is a new version, not a moved tag. The stop rows of the table are for a human: find out where the image, the asset or the release came from, and release a higher version.
One rule governs every publishing step: **a published artifact is never replaced, and it is reused only once it is proven to be this run's**, never because something with the right name exists.

**The image.** A new image is copied to GHCR by digest with no tag, attested and signed, and only then tagged `:<version>`, so a version tag only ever points at a digest this workflow tested, scanned, attested and signed. An untagged digest left by a failed run is inert. A reused image must pass `gh attestation verify oci://…@<digest> … --source-ref refs/heads/master --source-digest <commit>` and carry this workflow's own cosign signature (identity `https://github.com/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml@refs/heads/master`, issuer `https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com`), both checked by `release-mode` first.

**The release assets.** The release is created as a draft if it does not exist. Each expected asset (the two binaries and `checksums.txt`) is inventoried one by one: a present asset is downloaded and compared by sha256 with this run's (the rebuilt or verified binary), and with the published `checksums.txt` when that is present, and a mismatch fails the run; a missing asset is uploaded, never with `--clobber`. An asset that is not expected fails the run. `checksums.txt` is regenerated over the final binaries, and must equal a published one.

**The binary attestations.** The binaries are the same bytes on every run, so an attestation an earlier run made for one is reused, not duplicated. `binary-attestation-status` looks up each binary's sha256: one with no attestation is attested; one with an attestation must pass `gh attestation verify <binary> … --source-ref refs/heads/master --source-digest <commit>` and is then left alone. Any other answer stops the run before the release is drafted, for a human.

**The latest pointers.** `:latest`, `:<major>` and the GitHub "Latest" marker move only if the version is still the highest when that pointer is moved: the highest remote tag is read again immediately before retagging the image, and again immediately before the release is published out of draft.

The last one is **best-effort, not atomic**. GHCR tags and GitHub releases cannot be updated together, so a tag created outside this workflow in the seconds between the two moves can still leave them disagreeing. The run then warns rather than moving anything back. Re-dispatch the higher version, whose own late checks repoint them, or retag by hand after checking the digest:

IMAGE=ghcr.io/leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter
DIGEST=sha256:...   # the digest of the image that should be latest
gh attestation verify "oci://$IMAGE@$DIGEST" --repo leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter \
  --signer-workflow leinardi/swarm-scheduler-exporter/.github/workflows/release.yaml --source-ref refs/heads/master
docker buildx imagetools create -t "$IMAGE:latest" -t "$IMAGE:<major>" "$IMAGE@$DIGEST"

A release is scanned once, when it is built, but vulnerabilities keep being published. [`.github/workflows/scheduled-scan.yaml`](../.github/workflows/scheduled-scan.yaml) runs every Monday, and on demand from the Actions tab. It resolves `:latest` to its index digest once and scans the `linux/amd64` and `linux/arm64` images by their own digests with the release's gate (`trivy-gate`, the latest Trivy, the same ignore file), and runs `make rust-deny` over `master`'s dependencies. Any finding fails the run. The published image is immutable, so the fix is a new release (for a base finding, on the base tag's newer rebuild), or a reviewed entry in the ignore file.

**Every action is pinned to a full commit SHA**, with the version in a trailing comment, in every workflow; Dependabot's `github-actions` ecosystem updates the pins. A tag is a mutable pointer, and an action that moved would execute inside the release job, which holds `contents: write`, `packages: write` and an OIDC identity. The one tool deliberately not pinned is Trivy, which `trivy-gate` installs at its latest release so every scan runs the newest checks (`meta/tests/toolchain.rs` fails on a Trivy pin). svu, ShellCheck, zig, cargo-zigbuild and cargo-deny are pinned with their checksums inside the gh-composite-actions that install them.

**Every image the release job runs is pinned by digest**: the job-local registry and skopeo in the workflow's `env`, the QEMU emulator and the Dockerfile frontend (`# syntax=…@sha256:…`). Bump them by hand, resolving a new digest with `docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>:<tag>`. **The `dhi.io` bases are pinned by tag, deliberately not by digest**, because dhi.io rebuilds its tags too often: `dhi.io/rust` for the default target's build stage and `dhi.io/static` for the shipped base, each in one literal `FROM <image>:<tag>` with an explicit tag other than `latest` (`meta/tests/dockerfiles.rs`, `check-pinned-bases`). Each release records the base digest it shipped (see [What CI proves](#what-ci-proves)). Dependabot's `docker` ecosystem moves the `dhi.io/static` tag; the `dhi.io/rust` tag is bumped by hand with `RUST_VERSION`, the `rust-std` digests and `rust-toolchain.toml` (the `toolchain` meta-test fails when the Rust line, the image patch or the copies of a zig pin disagree).

**The binaries are built outside Docker, once.** The release's `rust-release-binaries` gets zig and cargo-zigbuild from gh-composite-actions' `setup-zigbuild`, at the versions the Makefile pins and the Dockerfile's build stage copies (`ZIG_VERSION`, `CARGO_ZIGBUILD_VERSION`), and refuses any other release on `PATH`; Rust comes from `rust-toolchain.toml` (`rustup toolchain install`), or, on a recovery, the release the tag records. The image's `prebuilt` target never runs that build stage: it COPYs the binaries, so `dhi.io/rust` is not part of a release at all.

**Workflow tokens are read-only by default.** Each workflow sets `permissions: contents: read` at the top; only the release job adds `contents: write`, `packages: write`, `id-token: write`, `attestations: write` and `actions: read` (to read the `audit` job), in the `release` environment, `ci-green` adds `actions: read`, and the reviewdog jobs in `ci.yaml` add `pull-requests: write` to post their review. The warm-up's calling job adds `actions: write`, so the reusable workflow's prune job can delete the older pre-commit caches of its ref.

**Caches.** The release's Rust build cache is its own (`prefix-key: release`), restored and saved only by this workflow, which runs on `master` only; CI's (`shared-key: ci`) is saved only on `master`, so no pull request can seed a cache the release reads; `integration.yaml` saves its own (`shared-key: ci`, `key: integration`) on `master` only, too. A cache only speeds the build: the binaries come from `Cargo.lock` and the remapped, pinned toolchain either way, and a recovery checks them by sha256 against what was published. No image build uses a layer cache. The pre-commit cache is written only by the warm-up workflow, on `master`.

The release job runs in the `release` environment. Create and configure it **before the first dispatch**, dry runs included: a run that references a missing environment creates it with no protection rules.

**Restrict it to `master`** with a deployment branch rule, as a server-side second line of defence behind the `guard` job. Add required reviewers too if a release should wait for a human. Leave the "Immutable tags" ruleset exactly as it is; the release job is written for it.
**The `dhi.io` token.** The image's base, `dhi.io/static`, cannot be pulled without a login (the user name is `leinardi`, written in the workflows), so three places need `DHI_TOKEN`:
the **release** job: an Actions secret, best **on the environment** (`gh secret set DHI_TOKEN --env release`), so only a job that passed the environment's rules reads it;
CI's **`image` job**, which runs on pull requests and pushes outside the environment: a repository Actions secret (`gh secret set DHI_TOKEN`);

**Dependabot**, which does not see Actions secrets: both to update the base (the `dhi` registry in [`.github/dependabot.yml`](../.github/dependabot.yml)) and for CI's `image` job on its pull requests (`gh secret set DHI_TOKEN -a dependabot`).
The `DHI_USERNAME` variable is no longer read.

A failing CI job does not block a merge on its own: the `master` ruleset needs a required status check for that. The rulesets are managed as code in [`leinardi/gh-leinardi-iac`](https://github.com/leinardi/gh-leinardi-iac), in the `repo_swarm_scheduler_exporter` module of `stacks/github-repos/repos.tf`, never by hand or with `gh api`: a change to them is a pull request there.

The checks to require are `ci-result` and `integration`, set there as `default_branch_required_checks = ["ci-result", "integration"]`. `ci-result` needs every other job of `ci.yaml` (`pre-commit-all`, `conventional-commits`, `rust` and `image`) and fails unless each one succeeded; `conventional-commits` alone may be skipped, off pull requests. A new `ci.yaml` job therefore becomes required by joining `ci-result`'s `needs`, not the ruleset, and GitHub counting a skipped required job as passing is why the jobs themselves are not listed. `integration` runs in its own workflow, which `ci-result` cannot need, so it is required by name. The reviewdog annotation jobs (`actionlint`, `pre-commit-hooks`, `markdownlint`, `shellcheck`, `yamllint`) stay optional: they duplicate `pre-commit-all` as inline comments. None of these workflows uses path filters, so every required check reports on every pull request.
The release does not depend on the rule: it reads `ci-result` of the commit's `ci.yaml` push run and `integration` of its `integration.yaml` push run itself (`require-ci-green`, once for each).

Once the ruleset is applied, open one pull request and confirm the required checks report under exactly the names `ci-result` and `integration`. A required check that never reports blocks every merge.
Repository admins keep the ruleset's pull-request bypass, so an admin can still merge a pull request whose check fails. That is a deliberate escape hatch, not a gap in the check.

One exact Rust release builds everything: `rust-toolchain.toml` (which the workflows install with `rustup toolchain install`, so they name no release of their own) and the `dhi.io/rust:<version>-debian13-dev` tag of the Dockerfile's build stage, and `meta/tests/toolchain.rs` fails when they differ, patch included. Dependabot ignores the `rust` image on purpose: `dhi.io/rust` has no rustup, so the build stage adds each musl target by unpacking `rust-std-<version>-<triple>.tar.xz` from static.rust-lang.org and checking it against a sha256 written in the Dockerfile, and those archives must be the image's exact release. A bump is therefore one hand-made pull request that moves, together:
the image tag and `ARG RUST_VERSION` in the Dockerfile;
the two `rust-std` sha256s in the Dockerfile (the `.sha256` file published next to each archive);
`RUST_RELEASE_RUST_STD_VERSION` and the same two sha256s in the Makefile;
`rust-toolchain.toml`;
the MSRV in `Cargo.toml` when the minor version changes.

zig and cargo-zigbuild follow the same rule between the Makefile (the one record of their versions and archive digests), the Dockerfile and the `setup-zigbuild` steps of `ci.yaml` and `release.yaml` (their `zig-version` and `cargo-zigbuild-version` inputs): each version is one value, and each digest one value between the Makefile and the Dockerfile, checked by the same meta-test. The Makefile's `RUST_RELEASE_*` settings override the defaults of the shared `.mk/rust-release.mk`, which is fetched from make-common and never edited here. gh-composite-actions' `setup-zigbuild` checks the archives it downloads against its `zig-sha256` and `cargo-zigbuild-sha256` inputs, whose defaults are its default versions' digests, so a version bump passes the new digests to it too. A release built after such a bump produces new binary digests, as any toolchain change does; a recovery of an older release must run on its own commit, which still names its own toolchain.

heading_path: Commit messages are checked on every pull request
blocks.text: Every commit must be a Conventional Commit with a scope (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#commit-messages)). The local `commit-msg` hook only runs where somebody ran `make pre-commit-install`, so a commit made without it would otherwise reach `master` unchecked. The `conventional-commits` job in [`.github/workflows/ci.yaml`](../.github/workflows/ci.yaml) closes that gap: on every pull request it runs the repository's own `conventional-pre-commit` hook, `--force-scope` included, over every commit between the pull request's base and head. Merge commits are skipped.

heading_path: Commit messages are checked on every pull request
blocks.text: Only merge commits are enabled on this repository; squash and rebase merging are disabled. Every commit in a pull request therefore lands on `master` as it is, and the pull-request title never becomes a commit subject, which is why there is no title check. If squash merging is ever enabled, the title becomes the commit subject, and a pull-request title check has to be added to CI first.
Releases up to and including `v1.3.2` were built from the Go implementation, which the 2.0 cutover replaced. What differed then, for anyone recovering or auditing one of them:

The binaries were built by `go build` with `CGO_ENABLED=0`, `-trimpath` and `-buildvcs=false`, the version stamped through `-ldflags -X`, and the Go version taken from `go.mod`; the image's build stage was `dhi.io/golang`.
The `test` job ran `make go-vet` and `go test -race ./...`, and the `audit` job ran govulncheck; CI's required `ci-result` also needed `repo-gates`, `go-test` and `go-vulncheck`.
`svu` was installed with `go install`, and the Go module and build caches were restored by `actions/setup-go`.
Dependabot's `gomod` updates were the dependency bumps committed as `fix(deps)`.
A recovery of a 1.x release runs on that release's commit, whose workflows still describe all of this, so nothing in this section is needed to run one.
